Your task is to complete formatter_agent. # In agent.py from datetime import datetime from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.tools import google_search # --- Custom Tools (Provided) --- def format_research_notes(topic: str, findings: str) -> dict: """Formats research findings into a structured document.""" timestamp = datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') document = f""" # Research Report: {topic} Generated: {timestamp} ## Findings {findings} """.strip() return {"status": "success", "document": document} def extract_key_facts(text: str, num_facts: int = 5) -> dict: """Extracts key sentences from a block of text.""" sentences = text.split('.') facts = [s.strip() for s in sentences if len(s.strip()) > 10][:num_facts] return {"status": "success", "facts": facts} # --- Agent 1: Search Specialist (Provided) --- # Only google_search -- it cannot be mixed with the custom tools below. research_agent = Agent( model='gemini-3.8-flash', name='research_agent', instruction=( "You are a research assistant. Use google_search to find current " "information on the topic you're given, then summarize the key " "findings in a few plain-text sentences." ), tools=[google_search], ) # --- Agent 2: Formatter --- # TODO: Define `formatter_agent`. # 1. Use 'gemini-3.8-flash'. # 2. Add `extract_key_facts` and `format_research_notes` to tools (do NOT # add google_search here -- that's the whole point of splitting these up). # 3. Write an instruction telling it to: first call extract_key_facts on the # findings text it's given, then call format_research_notes with the # topic and those facts, then present the final document as its answer. formatter_agent = Agent(...)
If you get stuck, you can find the complete, working code in the lab-solution.md file.

You have successfully built a two-agent pipeline that bridges the knowledge gap of LLMs using built-in grounding tools. You have learned: How to easily enable web search using the google_search built-in tool. Why google_search can't share an agent with custom function tools, and how to work around that with sequential composition instead. How to write instructions that guide each agent through its own focused part of a larger research-and-formatting workflow.

Why is google_search considered a "built-in" tool while format_research_notes is a "custom" tool? What are the benefits of having the model perform the search inside its own environment rather than you writing a Python script to scrape Google results? main.py passes findings between the two agents as a plain string. What would you have to change if you instead wanted formatter_agent to be able to ask research_agent follow-up questions?

This file contains the complete code for agent.py and main.py in the Research Assistant lab: two agents, called in sequence, since google_search can't share an agent with custom function tools.

""" Research Assistant with Web Grounding Searches web, extracts key information, and formats a report. """ from datetime import datetime from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.tools import google_search # --- Custom Tools --- def format_research_notes(topic: str, findings: str) -> dict: """Formats research findings into a structured document.""" timestamp = datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') document = f""" # Research Report: {topic} Generated: {timestamp} ## Findings {findings} """.strip() return {"status": "success", "document": document} def extract_key_facts(text: str, num_facts: int = 5) -> dict: """Extracts key sentences from a block of text.""" sentences = text.split('.') # Filter for meaningful sentences facts = [s.strip() for s in sentences if len(s.strip()) > 10][:num_facts] return {"status": "success", "facts": facts} # --- Agent 1: Search Specialist --- # Only google_search -- it cannot be mixed with custom function tools in the # same agent (a Gemini API restriction: a mixed tools list constructs fine in # Python but fails at the first real model call with # `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT: Multiple tools are supported only when they are all # search tools.`). research_agent = Agent( model='gemini-3.8-flash', name='research_agent', instruction=( "You are a research assistant. Use google_search to find current " "information on the topic you're given, then summarize the key " "findings in a few plain-text sentences." ), tools=[google_search], ) # --- Agent 2: Formatter --- # Only the custom tools -- no google_search here. formatter_agent = Agent( model='gemini-3.8-flash', name='formatter_agent', instruction=""" You are a report formatter. The user will give you a topic and some research findings as plain text. 1. Call extract_key_facts on the findings text to pull out the most important points. 2. Call format_research_notes with the topic and those facts to produce a final report. Present the final formatted document as your answer, verbatim. """, tools=[extract_key_facts, format_research_notes], )
Create the agent project: uv run adk create research_assistant cd research_assistant Configure .env for Vertex AI. Run the script: uv run python main.py

Why is google_search considered a "built-in" tool while format_research_notes is a "custom" tool? Answer: google_search runs inside Google's own infrastructure, invoked directly by the model with no code of yours executing -- Google built, hosts, and maintains it. format_research_notes is a plain Python function you wrote and control entirely; the ADK just exposes it to the model as a callable tool via its signature and docstring. What are the benefits of having the model perform the search inside its own environment rather than you writing a Python script to scrape Google results? Answer: google_search runs inside Google's own infrastructure, so you get results that are already fresh, ranked, and grounded -- no scraping code to write or maintain, no HTML to parse, no risk of a page layout change silently breaking your tool, and no separate API key or rate-limit budget to manage. It also stays legally and ethically clean (no ToS-violating scraping), and the model gets structured, citation-ready grounding metadata back instead of raw markup it would have to interpret itself. main.py passes findings between the two agents as a plain string. What would you have to change if you instead wanted formatter_agent to be able to ask research_agent follow-up questions? Answer: A one-way string handoff can't support a back-and-forth. You'd need formatter_agent to actually invoke research_agent as a tool call, not just receive its output as a static string -- for example, by wrapping research_agent as a sub-agent it can transfer control to and back, or by exposing a call_research_agent(question: str) function tool that internally runs research_agent and returns its answer. Either way, this pushes you from "sequential composition" into genuine multi-agent orchestration -- which is exactly what Module 15 covers next.

By now, you know how to build stateful tools using the ToolContext. But ToolContext is much more than just a window into the session state; it is your gateway to controlling the ADK Runtime itself. In this module, we will explore how to implement Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) safety and how tools can dynamically influence the agent's next steps.

Figure: Runtime dependency injection with ToolContext — state manipulation, audit trail, and execution lifecycle. To get access to the ToolContext, you simply add a special parameter to your tool function's signature: tool_context: ToolContext. from google.adk.tools import ToolContext def my_advanced_tool(some_argument: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict: # Now you can use tool_context inside your function ... When the agent calls your tool, the ADK framework will see this special parameter and automatically inject the ToolContext object for the current request. Important: You should not mention the tool_context parameter in your function's docstring. The LLM doesn't know or care about the context object; it's a mechanism for your code to interact with the ADK framework after the LLM has decided to call your tool.

For sensitive or destructive actions (like financial transfers, deleting files, or sending emails), you shouldn't trust the LLM to act alone. ADK 2.0 provides a native mechanism to pause execution and wait for a human "OK." To enable this, you must wrap your Python function in a FunctionTool object. from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool # Wrap the tool and enable confirmation secure_tool = FunctionTool( my_sensitive_function, require_confirmation=True # 🛡️ The safety trigger ) When the agent calls this tool, the ADK will: Pause the interaction. Send a RequestInput event to the user (via the Dev UI or API). Execute the Python code only if the user clicks "Approve."

Sometimes a tool needs to tell the framework: "Wait, don't just return my result to the agent; do something else first!" You do this via the actions attribute. Dynamic Agent Transfers​ A tool can decide to hand over the entire conversation to another specialist node in the graph. def check_emergency(level: int, tool_context: ToolContext): if level > 9: # 🏃 Dynamic hand-off tool_context.actions.transfer_to_agent = "emergency_specialist" return "Escalating to emergency support." return "All clear." Skipping Summarization​ If your tool returns a perfect, ready-to-use message for the user, you can prevent the LLM from rewriting it. tool_context.actions.skip_summarization = True

Tools can also interact with files uploaded by the user (like images, logs, or reports). def analyze_logs(file_name: str, tool_context: ToolContext): log_file = tool_context.load_artifact(file_name) if log_file: content = log_file.text # ... logic ... By leveraging the ToolContext, you can elevate your custom functions from simple calculators to powerful, context-aware components that are deeply integrated into the agent's lifecycle. [!NOTE] Pedagogical Note: Although we will dive deep into multi-agent orchestration and workflows on Day 3 (Module 15+), in the following lab we will use a simple, single-edge Workflow container. This is not a technical requirement — a plain Agent with sub_agents=[...] supports the same dynamic hand-off (transfer_to_agent) to a supervisor agent, with no Workflow wrapper needed. We use Workflow here purely as a stylistic choice, to keep the project structure consistent with the multi-agent patterns you'll build starting in Module 15. In the following lab, you will use human confirmation and workflow actions to build a secure financial escalation system.

HITL is a mandatory pattern for high-stakes enterprise agents. Use FunctionTool to add metadata and safety controls to your Python functions. tool_context.actions allows tools to steer the Workflow Runtime (Transfers, Skipping). Tools are "Framework Aware" components, not just isolated functions.

In this lab, you will build a Secure Finance Agent. You will learn how to implement Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) for sensitive transactions and how to use tool_context.actions to dynamically escalate a conversation to a supervisor node.

Use this tool only when the user explicitly asks to 'invest' or 'buy'. """ # 1. Check for escalation: Any amount > 10,000 needs a human supervisor if amount > 10000: # TODO: Set tool_context.actions.transfer_to_agent to "supervisor" # Hint: This will dynamically route the user to a different node. pass return f"Amount ${amount} requires supervisor approval. Escalating..." # 2. Regular investment logic return f"Success! ${amount} has been invested in your portfolio."

Exercise: Open agent.py. You need to wrap your tool in a FunctionTool to enable the confirmation pop-up. # In agent.py from google.adk import Agent, Workflow from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool from .tools.finance import execute_investment # --- 1. Define the Supervisor Node --- supervisor = Agent( name="supervisor", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="You are a senior supervisor. Review the large investment request and provide a final verdict." ) # --- 2. Wrap the Tool for Safety --- # TODO: Create a FunctionTool named 'secure_investment_tool' # Enable require_confirmation=True secure_investment_tool = ... # --- 3. Define the Main Agent --- finance_agent = Agent( name="finance_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="Help users with their investments. Use 'execute_investment' for trades.", tools=[secure_investment_tool], sub_agents=[supervisor] # Required for discovery during transfer ) # --- 4. Build the Workflow Graph --- root_agent = Workflow( name="SecureSystem", edges=[("START", finance_agent)] )

documents.t: Start the Dev UI: uv run adk web . Test HITL: Ask: "Invest $500 for me." Observe: A confirmation box should appear. The code only runs if you click "Approve." Test Dynamic Transfer: Ask: "Invest $50,000 for me." Observe: Since require_confirmation=True wraps the tool unconditionally, you will see the same confirmation pop-up as above first — click "Approve" to let the tool actually run. Only then does the escalation logic inside execute_investment fire. In the Trace, you will see the active_agent change from finance_agent to supervisor.

You have built a production-ready secure agent! You learned: How to pause execution for human approval using require_confirmation. How to reroute the conversation dynamically using tool_context.actions.transfer_to_agent. How to combine manual safety (HITL) with automated business rules (Escalation).

Record this lab as completed in your study plan? ✓ Mark as Complete Lab 13 Solution: Building a Secure Agent with HITL and Actions Goal​ This file contains the complete code for the finance.py and agent.py files using ADK 2.0 standards for advanced tool interactions. secure_finance/tools/finance.py​ from google.adk.tools import ToolContext def execute_investment(amount: float, tool_context: ToolContext) -> str: """ Executes a long-term investment. Use this tool only when the user explicitly asks to 'invest' or 'buy'. """ # Business Rule: Large amounts require senior supervisor review if amount > 10000: # 🏃 Dynamic Workflow Action: Hand-off to the supervisor node tool_context.actions.transfer_to_agent = "supervisor" return f"Investment of ${amount} exceeds local limit. Handing off to supervisor..." # Logic for standard investments return f"Success! ${amount} has been invested in your portfolio." secure_finance/agent.py​ from google.adk import Agent, Workflow from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool from .tools.finance import execute_investment # 1. Define the Specialist Node (Supervisor) supervisor = Agent( name="supervisor", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction=""" You are a senior investment supervisor. You have been called because a user wants to make a large investment (> $10,000). Review the request and the user's history, then provide a professional recommendation. """ ) # 2. Wrap the Tool for Safety (HITL) # We use FunctionTool to add the requirement for human confirmation. secure_investment_tool = FunctionTool( execute_investment, require_confirmation=True ) # 3. Define the Main Agent Node finance_agent = Agent( name="finance_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash", description="A secure finance assistant.", instruction=""" You are a helpful investment assistant. Use 'execute_investment' to help users trade. If the user wants to invest more than $10k, explain that you are escalating to a supervisor. """, tools=[secure_investment_tool], sub_agents=[supervisor] # Discovery for dynamic hand-off ) # 4. Build the Workflow Graph root_agent = Workflow( name="SecureSystem", edges=[("START", finance_agent)] ) Self-Reflection Answers​ Why is it more secure to use require_confirmation for sensitive actions rather than just relying on the LLM's instructions? Answer: Instructions are just "advice" to the LLM. Through prompt injection or adversarial inputs, a user could trick the model into skipping a step or ignoring a rule. require_confirmation is a hard-coded framework feature. The ADK literally will not call your Python function unless the user explicitly approves the action in the UI, providing a solid security guarantee. In the dynamic transfer example, why did we need to add the supervisor agent to the sub_agents list of the finance_agent? Answer: In ADK 2.0, an agent can only transfer to nodes it "knows" about. Adding an agent to the sub_agents list registers it as a valid destination in the local graph. Without this registration, the transfer_to_agent action would fail because the framework wouldn't be able to find the target node. How does tool_context.actions allow you to implement business rules that the LLM cannot override? Answer: Because the actions are processed by the Python runtime, not the LLM. When our code sets transfer_to_agent, the ADK intercepts this and forces the transition. The LLM doesn't even get to see the result of the tool before the hand-off happens, ensuring the business logic (like the $10,000 limit) is strictly enforced.

documents.s: Module 13.5: Extending ADK - Custom Persistence with Firestore

documents.t: One of the key strengths of ADK 2.0 is its pluggable architecture. While the core library provides built-in services for common tasks (like InMemorySessionService or DatabaseSessionService for SQL), enterprise requirements often demand integration with specific technologies. Instead of being locked into a fixed set of database providers, you can extend the ADK by implementing your own services.

Figure: Cloud-native session synchronization — event persistence, state delta loading, and atomic cloud commits with Google Cloud Firestore. In the ADK, all session persistence is governed by a single abstract class: BaseSessionService. Any class that inherits from BaseSessionService and implements its core methods can be used by the Runner. This allows you to store agent conversations and state in any database—from Redis and MongoDB to Google Cloud Firestore.

Organizational Standards: Your company may already use Firestore as its primary serverless database. Performance & Latency: You might need sub-second latency for a high-traffic customer bot. In this case, you could implement a custom service using Redis to cache session state in-memory, ensuring near-instant response times that a standard persistent database might not provide. Specific Features: You might want to leverage Firestore's real-time listeners or its native integration with Firebase. Cost & Scaling: Firestore offers a specialized pricing model and automatic scaling that might be better suited for your agent's traffic patterns than a traditional SQL database.
documents.s: Why Implement a Custom Session Service?

documents.t: The ADK uses Dependency Injection at the Runner level. When you instantiate a Runner, you don't have to use the default InMemoryRunner. Instead, you can provide your own custom session service instance. # Custom implementation (which we will build in this lab) custom_service = FirestoreSessionService(project_id="my-project") # Inject it into the base Runner runner = Runner( app=my_app, session_service=custom_service ) From this point on, every call to runner.run() or runner.run_async() will automatically use your Firestore logic to save and load data, without you having to change a single line of agent instruction or tool code.

ADK is extensible: You can plug in custom implementations for sessions, artifacts, and more. Decoupled Logic: Your agent's "brain" (intelligence) is completely separated from its "memory" (storage technology). Enterprise Ready: Building custom providers is the standard way to integrate ADK into existing enterprise data ecosystems.

In this lab, you will learn how to extend the ADK's core functionality by implementing a Custom Session Service. You will take a specialized FirestoreSessionService implementation and "plug it in" to an agent's runtime. By the end of this lab, you will have an agent that persists its memory to Google Cloud Firestore, surviving restarts of the Python process.

Create a file named firestore_provider.py. This contains the implementation that inherits from BaseSessionService. Study the code to see how it uses firestore.AsyncClient to map ADK concepts (Apps, Users, Sessions) to document paths. # firestore_provider.py from typing import Any, Optional import uuid import time from google.cloud import firestore from google.adk.sessions.base_session_service import BaseSessionService, GetSessionConfig, ListSessionsResponse from google.adk.sessions.session import Session from google.adk.events.event import Event class FirestoreSessionService(BaseSessionService): def __init__(self, project_id: str): self._client = firestore.AsyncClient(project=project_id) async def create_session(self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, state: Optional[dict] = None, session_id: Optional[str] = None) -> Session: sid = session_id or str(uuid.uuid4()) # Reference: apps/{app}/users/{user}/sessions/{sid} session_ref = self._client.collection("apps").document(app_name)\ .collection("users").document(user_id)\ .collection("sessions").document(sid) # Check if exists, else create doc = await session_ref.get() if not doc.exists: await session_ref.set({ "created_at": time.time(), "state": state or {} }) return Session(id=sid, app_name=app_name, user_id=user_id, state=doc.to_dict().get("state", {}) if doc.exists else (state or {})) async def get_session(self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, session_id: str, config: Optional[GetSessionConfig] = None) -> Optional[Session]: session_ref = self._client.collection("apps").document(app_name)\ .collection("users").document(user_id)\ .collection("sessions").document(session_id) doc = await session_ref.get() if not doc.exists: return None # Rebuild the event history from the events sub-collection -- this is # what actually gives the agent its memory across separate script # runs. Returning state alone (without events) isn't enough: the # model recalls prior turns from conversation history, not just the # state dict. events = [] async for event_doc in session_ref.collection("events").order_by("timestamp").stream(): events.append(Event.model_validate(event_doc.to_dict())) return Session( id=session_id, app_name=app_name, user_id=user_id, state=doc.to_dict().get("state", {}), events=events, ) async def append_event(self, session: Session, event: Event) -> Event: # Let the base implementation apply event.actions.state_delta to # session.state in-memory first (it also handles temp-scoped state # and trims it before we persist) -- without this, state changes are # silently dropped: they'd never make it past this method. event = await super().append_event(session=session, event=event) # Save event to sub-collection event_ref = self._client.collection("apps").document(session.app_name)\ .collection("users").document(session.user_id)\ .collection("sessions").document(session.id)\ .collection("events").document(event.invocation_id) await event_ref.set(event.model_dump()) print(f"🔥 [Firestore] Persisted event from {event.author}") # Persist the now-updated state too, so a fresh get_session() call # (e.g. from a new process) sees it. await self.update_session_state(session) return event async def update_session_state(self, session: Session) -> None: # Update the main session document's state session_ref = self._client.collection("apps").document(session.app_name)\ .collection("users").document(session.user_id)\ .collection("sessions").document(session.id) await session_ref.update({"state": session.state}) print(f"🔥 [Firestore] Updated session state in cloud.") # Mandatory stubs for BaseSessionService async def list_sessions(self, *, app_name: str, user_id: Optional[str] = None) -> ListSessionsResponse: return ListSessionsResponse(sessions=[]) async def delete_session(self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, session_id: str) -> None: pass

While the ADK provides a powerful framework for building custom tools, you don't always have to reinvent the wheel. The AI and Python ecosystems are vast, with many open-source libraries that already provide pre-built tools for a wide range of tasks. Frameworks like LangChain have a rich ecosystem of "toolkits" and "agents" that come with ready-to-use integrations for services like Wikipedia, WolframAlpha, various search APIs, and more. The Google ADK is designed with interoperability in mind. It allows you to tap into this vast ecosystem by providing simple wrappers that make it possible to use tools from other popular frameworks directly within your ADK agent. This lets you leverage the best of both worlds: the robust, scalable architecture of the ADK and the extensive tool library of the broader community.
documents.s: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants

documents.t: Figure: The ADK third-party wrapper pipeline — adapting external framework tools (LangChain, CrewAI) into native ADK CallableTool contracts. The key to this integration is the Wrapper Pattern. The ADK provides special wrapper classes, like LangchainTool, that act as adapters. Here's how it works: You find a tool you want to use from a third-party library (e.g., a Wikipedia search tool from LangChain). You instantiate this third-party tool according to its own library's documentation. You "wrap" this instance inside the corresponding ADK wrapper class (e.g., LangchainTool(tool=your_langchain_tool_instance)). You add the wrapped tool to your ADK agent's tools list. The ADK wrapper handles all the translation behind the scenes. It inspects the third-party tool, extracts its name, description, and parameters, and generates the necessary schema for the Gemini LLM to understand it. When the LLM decides to call the tool, the wrapper receives the request, calls the underlying third-party tool's execution method, and then formats the result back into a standard dictionary that the ADK agent can understand. Once wrapped, a third-party tool behaves just like a custom function tool you wrote yourself — you can freely mix multiple wrapped tools (e.g. a WikipediaQueryRun from LangChain alongside your own get_order_status function) in the same agent's tools list. Important restriction: As Module 12 covered, a built-in tool like google_search cannot share an agent's tools list with any custom function tools — and a wrapped third-party tool counts as a custom function tool for this purpose. This is a restriction from the Gemini API itself (not the ADK): it constructs fine in Python but fails the moment the model actually runs, with 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT: Multiple tools are supported only when they are all search tools. So an agent can have google_search or a mix of custom/third-party tools, but not both together. If you need grounding and a third-party tool like Wikipedia search in the same system, use the same sequential composition pattern from Module 12: run a google_search-only agent, then feed its output into a second agent that has your wrapped third-party tool(s).

Saves Development Time: Instead of writing your own code to connect to the Wikipedia API, you can use a pre-built, tested, and maintained tool from a library like LangChain in just a few lines of code. Access to a Huge Library: You gain immediate access to hundreds of existing tools for a massive variety of tasks. Focus on Your Core Logic: You can spend your time building the unique tools and business logic that are specific to your application, while relying on the community for common, general-purpose tools. In the lab for this module, you will put this into practice by integrating a powerful web search tool from the LangChain ecosystem into your ADK agent.

The ADK is interoperable and can integrate tools from third-party libraries like LangChain. The ADK uses a "Wrapper Pattern" (e.g., LangchainTool) to adapt third-party tools for use within an ADK agent. This approach saves significant development time by allowing you to leverage a vast ecosystem of pre-built, community-maintained tools. Potential Risk: Integrating third-party libraries, especially those with extensive dependencies (like LangChain), can introduce the risk of "dependency conflicts" (often called "dependency hell"), where different libraries require incompatible versions of the same underlying package. A wrapped third-party tool counts as a custom function tool, so it can freely mix with your own function tools — but, as in Module 12, it still cannot share a tools list with a built-in tool like google_search; use sequential composition if you need both. This wraps up Part 2: Tools & Capabilities — your agent can now search, remember, call your own functions, and borrow tools from an entire ecosystem. In Part 3, you'll learn how to coordinate multiple specialized agents into Multi-Agent Systems.

documents.t: Because we are importing Python objects, we need to define our agent in a Python file. Exercise: Create a new file named agent.py. Inside this file, complete the # TODO items to build the agent. You will need to instantiate the LangChain tool, wrap it, and then define your agent to use the wrapped tool. Heads-up: Wikipedia now requires a distinctive User-Agent. Wikimedia rate-limits the generic default User-Agent string that the wikipedia package sends (it's shared by every user of the package, so Wikimedia throttles it collectively). Without a fix, calls to the tool fail with a requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError. The fix is one line: call wikipedia.set_user_agent("your-app-name/1.0 (contact-info)") once, before the tool makes any requests. It's already included in the starter code below. # In agent.py (Starter Code) from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.integrations.langchain import LangchainTool import wikipedia from langchain_community.tools import WikipediaQueryRun from langchain_community.utilities import WikipediaAPIWrapper # Wikimedia now rate-limits the wikipedia package's generic default User-Agent. # Set a distinctive one before making any requests. wikipedia.set_user_agent("adk-training-fact-finder/1.0 (https://github.com/adk-training; contact@example.com)") # TODO: 1. Instantiate the LangChain tool. # - Create a WikipediaAPIWrapper. # - Create a WikipediaQueryRun instance using the wrapper. # (Refer to LangChain documentation if needed). langchain_tool_instance = None # TODO: 2. Wrap the LangChain tool instance with the ADK's `LangchainTool` wrapper. wikipedia_tool = None # TODO: 3. Define the `root_agent` as an `Agent`. # - Give it a name, model (`gemini-3.8-flash`), and description. # - Write an instruction to use the Wikipedia tool for factual questions. # - Add your wrapped `wikipedia_tool` to its `tools` list. root_agent = Agent( name="fact_finder_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash", description="An agent that can look up information on Wikipedia.", instruction="""# Your instruction here...""", tools=[ # Your tools here... ] )

Delete the placeholder root_agent.yaml file, as your agent is now defined in agent.py. rm root_agent.yaml Set up your .env file with your API key. Run the agent: uv run adk web fact_finder_agent The ADK will automatically find the root_agent object in your agent.py file.

documents.t: Interact with the agent in the Dev UI. Ask it questions that require an encyclopedia: "Who was Marie Curie?" "What is the theory of relativity?" Examine the Trace View to confirm that the WikipediaQueryRun tool was called. If the tool call still fails with a network or JSON error even after setting the User-Agent, wait a few seconds and try again. Wikimedia occasionally rate-limits shared or cloud IP ranges (like Cloud Shell or CI runners) regardless of a correctly-set User-Agent -- this is a separate, transient issue from the User-Agent fix above, and it usually clears up on retry.
If you get stuck, you can find the complete, working code in the lab-solution.md file.

According to LangChain documentation, instantiate the tool. # This sets up the connection to the Wikipedia API. api_wrapper = WikipediaAPIWrapper(top_k_results=1, doc_content_chars_max=2000) langchain_tool_instance = WikipediaQueryRun(api_wrapper=api_wrapper) # 2. Wrap the LangChain tool instance with the ADK's LangchainTool wrapper. # The wrapper automatically inspects the tool and creates the schema for the LLM. wikipedia_tool = LangchainTool(tool=langchain_tool_instance) # 3. Define the ADK agent and include the wrapped tool in its tools list. root_agent = Agent( name="fact_finder_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash", description="An agent that can look up information on Wikipedia.", instruction="""You are a helpful fact-finding assistant. If the user asks a question about a specific topic, person, or event, you MUST use the Wikipedia tool to find an accurate answer. Summarize the information you find in a clear and concise way.""", tools=[wikipedia_tool] ) Running the Agent​ Because this agent is defined in a Python file, you must delete the placeholder root_agent.yaml file from the project directory before running uv run adk web. Self-Reflection Answers​ The LangchainTool wrapper works by inspecting the LangChain tool object. What attributes do you think the wrapper is looking for on the LangChain tool to automatically generate the schema for the ADK agent? Answer: The wrapper typically looks for attributes like .name, .description (or .desc), and sometimes the input schema or .args definition of the LangChain tool. It uses these to construct the function declaration that the LLM (Gemini) requires, effectively translating the LangChain tool definition into the format expected by the ADK's function calling mechanism. Besides Wikipedia, what other pre-built tools from the LangChain ecosystem can you find that would be useful to integrate into an ADK agent? Answer: The LangChain ecosystem is vast. Some other highly useful tools include: DuckDuckGoSearchRun: For general web search (alternative to Google Search). PythonREPL: For executing Python code (though ADK has its own executors, this is a common one). WolframAlphaQueryRun: For advanced mathematical and scientific computations. ArxivQueryRun: For searching academic papers. RequestsGetTool: For making generic HTTP GET requests. What are the potential downsides or risks of relying on third-party, community-maintained tools in a production application? Answer: Risks include: Maintenance & Stability: Community tools might be abandoned, have breaking changes in updates, or have bugs that aren't quickly fixed. Security: You are trusting the code within that library. A malicious update or a vulnerability in the tool could compromise your agent. Dependency Conflicts: As mentioned in the module theory, adding large libraries like LangChain can introduce "dependency hell," where different parts of your application require incompatible versions of the same underlying package. Control: You have less control over exactly how the tool works compared to a custom function you wrote yourself.

🧭 Where We Are in Part 3: Welcome to Part 3: Multi-Agent Systems! Here in Chapter A (Modules 15–16), we start with LLM-Driven Agent Teams, where a coordinator Agent dynamically delegates work to specialist sub_agents. Later in Chapter B (Modules 17–20), you will build deterministic and programmable workflows where your graph and Python code control the exact execution order. Figure: Architectural transition from monolithic agent bottlenecks to distributed, specialized Multi-Agent Systems.

So far, you've built single, specialized agents. This is a great start, but the true power of the ADK is unlocked when you begin to compose multiple agents into a Multi-Agent System (MAS). As applications grow, trying to pack all the logic, tools, and instructions into a single monolithic agent becomes difficult to manage, debug, and scale. Imagine a customer support bot that needs to handle billing, technical support, and sales. A single agent trying to do all of this would have an incredibly complex instruction prompt and a confusing mix of tools. A much better approach is to break down the problem.

Figure: Structural breakdown of a single monolithic agent versus a decomposed multi-agent team with clean cognitive boundaries. A multi-agent system is an application where different, specialized agents collaborate to achieve a larger goal. Instead of one agent that does everything, you create a team of experts: One agent is an expert in billing. Another is an expert in technical support. A third is an expert in sales. And a "manager" or "coordinator" agent whose only job is to understand the user's initial request and route it to the correct specialist. This design pattern offers significant advantages: Modularity: Each agent is a self-contained unit with a clear purpose. Its instructions and tools are focused on a single domain. Maintainability: If you need to update the billing logic, you only need to modify the billing agent, without any risk of breaking the technical support functionality. Reusability: A well-defined "Billing Agent" can be reused in other applications across your organization. Scalability: It's easier to reason about and scale a system of smaller, collaborating components than one giant, complex agent.
documents.s: The Power of Specialization and Collaboration

documents.t: In ADK 2.0, every multi-agent architecture falls into one of three clear families, which you will master step by step across Part 3: Chapter Modules Who Controls Routing? Core Pattern When to Choose It A. LLM-Driven Agent Teams 15 – 16 Gemini decides dynamically based on specialist descriptions Coordinator Agent + sub_agents & collaboration modes Conversational triage, open-ended requests, interactive sub-tasks. B. Graph & Code Workflows 17 – 20 Your graph / Python code decides deterministically Sequential/parallel pipelines, Python orchestrators, dictionary switches, loops Fixed business steps, parallel fan-out/fan-in, multi-step Python logic, iterative refinement. C. Distributed MAS 21 Cross-service network calls over HTTP Remote network proxy agents & tool wrappers Agents owned by separate teams or running as independent microservices.

documents.t: Let's start with the simplest, most intuitive pattern — LLM-Driven Delegation using sub_agents: Define Specialist Agents: Create focused Agent instances, giving each one a crisp, action-oriented description. Define a Coordinator (root_agent): Pass your specialists into the coordinator's sub_agents=[...] list. Automatic Hand-off Under the Hood: ADK inspects every specialist's name and description and automatically injects a built-in transfer_to_agent capability into the coordinator. At runtime, Gemini reads the user's message, matches it against the specialists' descriptions, and hands off the conversation to the right expert! from google.adk import Agent # 1. Define Specialist Agents (each with a clear `description` for discovery) billing_expert = Agent( name="billing_expert", model="gemini-3.8-flash", description="Handles invoices, refunds, and payment questions.", instruction="You are a billing specialist. Help the user with payment issues.", ) tech_support = Agent( name="tech_support", model="gemini-3.8-flash", description="Handles bugs, login errors, and technical troubleshooting.", instruction="You are a technical support engineer. Diagnose and resolve technical issues.", ) # 2. Define the Coordinator as root_agent and register specialists via `sub_agents` root_agent = Agent( name="support_router", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction=( "Triage the user's request and transfer it to the appropriate specialist: " "'billing_expert' for payment issues or 'tech_support' for technical problems. " "If neither applies, answer politely yourself." ), sub_agents=[billing_expert, tech_support], ) Why description matters so much: Notice that support_router does not guess blindly — Gemini relies directly on each sub-agent's description to decide which specialist matches the user's intent. Writing clear, non-overlapping descriptions is one of the most important skills in MAS design. All agents in the same session also share ctx.session.state, so any structured data saved via output_key (from Module 04) remains accessible across the team. 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer In an ADK 2.0 multi-agent team using `sub_agents=[...]`, what is the primary role of each specialist agent's `description` parameter? AGemini reads each sub-agent's description (via ADK's built-in transfer mechanism) to decide which specialist matches the user's requestBIt forces all specialist agents to execute in parallel synchronously on every turnCIt merges all specialist tools into a single shared prompt templateDIt disables session state sharing between specialist agents Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

documents.t: Three MAS Families: Part 3 progresses from LLM-driven sub_agents teams (15–16) to deterministic/programmable Workflow graphs (17–20) to distributed A2A services (21). Specialization is Key: Each agent should have a narrow, well-defined domain and toolset. sub_agents + description: Registering specialists in sub_agents enables automatic LLM-driven hand-offs guided by each specialist's description.

In this lab, you will build and run your first live Multi-Agent System (MAS) using ADK 2.0's sub_agents delegation pattern: A router_agent (root_agent) whose sole job is to understand which language the user wants and transfer the conversation to the matching specialist. Two domain specialists — spanish_greeter_agent and japanese_greeter_agent — isolated in their own module (specialists.py) with crisp, non-overlapping description strings.

User Prompt Expected Flow "Can you greet me in Spanish?" router_agent transfers to spanish_greeter_agent → replies warmly in Spanish ("¡Hola!..."). "Please greet me in Japanese." router_agent transfers to japanese_greeter_agent → replies politely in Japanese. "Greet me in French!" router_agent sees no matching specialist in sub_agents → politely explains French isn't supported yet.

Environment setup: 1-Click Launch (Browser): Open in GitHub CodespacesOpen in Google Cloud Shell Local machine: If you're continuing the course in sequence, cd into the adk-training project you created in Module 2 and skip the block below -- your environment and dependencies already carry forward. If you're starting fresh at this module, create that project first: uv init adk-training --python 3.10 && cd adk-training uv add "google-adk>=2.1.0" python-dotenv DevContainer / Codespaces (Alternative): If you opened this repository in a DevContainer or GitHub Codespaces, Python 3.11, uv, gcloud, and all core ADK dependencies are pre-installed in your container environment. From your main adk-training directory, scaffold a new agent project: uv run adk create greeting_system Your folder structure will look like this once you add specialists.py: adk-training/ └── greeting_system/ ├── .env ├── __init__.py ├── specialists.py <-- Step 2: Specialist sub-agents └── agent.py <-- Step 3: Coordinator (root_agent)

Create greeting_system/specialists.py and complete the TODO placeholders. Remember: the coordinator's LLM reads each specialist's description to decide whom to transfer to! # greeting_system/specialists.py from google.adk import Agent # TODO: Define spanish_greeter (name="spanish_greeter_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash") # - Write a clear `description` so the router knows it handles Spanish greetings. # - Write an `instruction` telling it to greet warmly ONLY in Spanish. spanish_greeter = Agent( name="spanish_greeter_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash", description=..., # TODO: Action-oriented description for discovery instruction=..., # TODO: Greet warmly in Spanish only ) # TODO: Define japanese_greeter (name="japanese_greeter_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash") # - Write a clear `description` so the router knows it handles Japanese greetings. # - Write an `instruction` telling it to greet politely ONLY in Japanese (with romaji). japanese_greeter = Agent( name="japanese_greeter_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash", description=..., # TODO: Action-oriented description for discovery instruction=..., # TODO: Greet politely in Japanese only )

Open greeting_system/agent.py and configure root_agent to delegate via sub_agents: # greeting_system/agent.py from google.adk import Agent from .specialists import spanish_greeter, japanese_greeter # TODO: Define root_agent (name="router_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash") # - Instruct it to delegate to the matching specialist in sub_agents (never greet in Spanish/Japanese itself), # and politely decline unsupported languages like French. # - Register both specialists in `sub_agents=[...]`. root_agent = Agent( name="router_agent", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction=..., # TODO: Triage instructions sub_agents=[...], # TODO: Register spanish_greeter and japanese_greeter )

Launch the Dev UI from your parent adk-training directory: uv run adk web (Select greeting_system from the agent dropdown). Test all three scenarios (Spanish, Japanese, and unsupported French). Check the Trace Tab: Expand the turn where you asked for Spanish — you will see router_agent automatically invoke transfer_to_agent(agent_name="spanish_greeter_agent"), followed immediately by spanish_greeter_agent generating the final reply!

How would you extend this team to support Italian greetings without rewriting the existing specialists? After router_agent transfers a conversation to spanish_greeter_agent, who handles the user's next message by default? Answer: By default (mode="chat"), spanish_greeter_agent stays active as the current conversational agent unless it decides to transfer back. 🧭 Where We Are in Part 3: In Module 15, your router_agent handed off the conversation to a specialist (sub_agents), and that specialist stayed active afterward (mode="chat"). Here in Module 16, we complete Chapter A (LLM-Driven Agent Teams) by learning how mode="single_turn" and mode="task" automatically return control to your coordinator so multiple specialists can collaborate on one plan! Figure: Native conversational hand-offs and collaboration modes between primary triage agents and specialized domain experts.
documents.s: Module 16: Collaborative Teams - Modes and Hand-offs

documents.t: When a coordinator needs input from two or more specialists to fulfill a single user request — for example, scouting an event venue and customizing a catering menu — a plain one-way hand-off isn't enough. You need a guarantee that each specialist finishes its job and hands the microphone back to the coordinator. ADK 2.0 solves this declaratively with Collaboration Modes.

When you register a sub-agent, the mode parameter controls who holds the microphone and when control returns to the coordinator: Mode Behavior Best For "chat" (default) Full hand-off. The sub-agent takes over the conversation and keeps control until it decides to transfer elsewhere. No automatic return. One-way triage transfers (like Module 15's Greeting Router or transferring permanently to a billing desk). "single_turn" Quick call-and-return. The sub-agent never talks directly to the user; it runs one reasoning step, returns the result, and the coordinator stays in control. Fast background lookups (e.g., checking venue capacity, querying a database) so the coordinator can combine multiple results. "task" Interactive sub-task with guaranteed return. The sub-agent can ask the user clarifying questions across as many turns as needed. Once finished, it calls ADK's built-in finish_task tool and control automatically returns to the coordinator in that same turn. Multi-turn sub-tasks (e.g., gathering dietary preferences for catering before handing back to the main event coordinator).

When a task-mode sub-agent pauses to ask the user a question and resumes on the next turn, ADK wakes up the dispatch chain. Because of this, every agent in a sub_agents chain using task mode must set rerun_on_resume=True: from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.tools import google_search # Specialist in 'task' mode: can ask the user questions, ground answers via Search, and return control automatically researcher = Agent( name="researcher", model="gemini-3.8-flash", mode="task", rerun_on_resume=True, tools=[google_search], instruction="Research the topic using google_search, ask clarifying questions if needed, and summarize.", ) # Coordinator: delegates to researcher and automatically regains control afterward root_agent = Agent( name="coordinator", model="gemini-3.8-flash", rerun_on_resume=True, sub_agents=[researcher], # ADK automatically injects delegation tools instruction="Delegate research to the specialist, then write a final conclusion.", ) Note (google_search Grounding): Equipping specialists with ADK's built-in google_search tool lets single_turn and task sub-agents retrieve live real-world facts (such as current weather forecasts or flight schedules) before handing control back to the coordinator. Using google_search requires a valid GOOGLE_API_KEY or an authenticated Vertex AI Google Cloud project.

Figure: Seamless control transfer pipeline preserving session memory, context serialization, and telemetry. When you list specialists in sub_agents=[...], ADK automatically injects delegation tools (such as transfer_to_agent or request_task_<agent_name>) into the coordinator: With default mode="chat", control transfers to the sub-agent; local sub-agents can choose to transfer back, but the framework does not enforce it. With mode="task" or mode="single_turn", returning control to the coordinator is guaranteed by the framework — so a coordinator can reliably consult multiple specialists in sequence and synthesize their answers. Alternative Tool Wrapper (AgentTool): ADK also provides AgentTool(agent=...) (from google.adk.tools.agent_tool), which wraps an agent inside tools=[...]. For local Python agents, ADK recommends preferring sub_agents with mode="single_turn" (and reserving AgentTool for external service proxies covered in Module 21). 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer Which Collaboration Mode allows a specialist sub-agent to ask the user follow-up questions across multiple turns and then automatically return control to the coordinator as soon as the sub-task is complete? Amode='chat'Bmode='single_turn'Cmode='task'Dmode='static' Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?
documents.s: 3. How Hand-offs Work Under the Hood

documents.t: Predictability: single_turn and task modes guarantee when and how control returns to your coordinator. Natural Conversation: Context and session history are preserved seamlessly across hand-offs. Cleaner Prompts: You don't need fragile prompt hacks telling sub-agents to "transfer back when done."

Collaboration Modes (chat, single_turn, task) control who holds the conversation and whether control returns automatically. Use mode="single_turn" for fast, non-interactive lookups and mode="task" for multi-turn sub-tasks with guaranteed return (finish_task). Set rerun_on_resume=True on every agent in a task-mode sub_agents chain.

In this lab, you will build a Travel Planning Team consisting of a Coordinator, a Weather Specialist, and a Flight Booker. You will learn how to use the mode parameter to create a system where sub-agents fulfill specific tasks and then automatically return control to the main planner.

Coordinator receives the user's travel request. It delegates to the Weather Specialist (in single_turn mode, equipped with google_search) to fetch a grounded real-world forecast. It then delegates to the Flight Booker (in task mode, also equipped with google_search) to look up real flight options and gather user preferences across multiple turns before returning control. Finally, the Coordinator synthesizes the complete travel plan. Important (google_search Grounding & Scope): Both specialists use ADK's built-in google_search tool (from google.adk.tools import google_search) so weather forecasts and flight schedule lookups return grounded real-world results. Running google_search requires a valid GOOGLE_API_KEY (or an authenticated Vertex AI GCP project). While flight options and schedules are looked up live via Google Search, actual ticket purchase/booking is of course simulated and never performed.

Flight lookups use live search grounding, while actual ticket booking is simulated and not performed.) from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.tools import google_search # 1. Define the Weather Specialist # We use 'single_turn' because this is a quick data retrieval task # with no need for further user interaction. weather_agent = Agent( name="weather_checker", model="gemini-3.8-flash", mode="single_turn", # Required on every agent in a sub_agents dispatch chain -- without it: # "ValueError: A node must have rerun_on_resume=True." rerun_on_resume=True, tools=[google_search], instruction=( "Use google_search to look up current weather conditions and provide " "a brief, grounded 3-day weather forecast for the user's destination." ), ) # 2. Define the Flight Booker # We use 'task' mode because the agent might need to ask # clarification questions before it considers its task "complete". flight_agent = Agent( name="flight_booker", model="gemini-3.8-flash", mode="task", # Required for any node that might pause and resume across turns -- # without it: "ValueError: A node must have rerun_on_resume=True." rerun_on_resume=True, tools=[google_search], instruction=""" Help the user find and select a flight. 1. Ask for their departure city, preferred airline, or departure time if not provided. 2. Use google_search to look up real-world flight routes and schedule options. 3. Once the user confirms their choice, summarize the selected flight details (simulated booking only -- no actual ticket is purchased) and finish the task. """, ) # 3. Define the Coordinator # The root agent manages the high-level flow. # It doesn't need a mode. root_agent = Agent( name="travel_planner", model="gemini-3.8-flash", # The coordinator itself also needs this -- it's part of the same # dispatch chain and can be "woken up" when a sub-agent's task resumes. rerun_on_resume=True, instruction=""" You are a travel planning coordinator. Your goal is to build a complete plan for the user. PROCESS: 1. Call `weather_checker` to get a grounded weather forecast. 2. Call `flight_booker` to research flight options and gather user preferences. 3. Once both sub-tasks are done, present a final cohesive travel summary to the user. """, sub_agents=[weather_agent, flight_agent], ) Self-Reflection Answers​ Why would you use single_turn instead of task for a database lookup specialist? Answer: Efficiency. single_turn is faster and cheaper because it forbids any further interaction. If a node's job is purely to fetch data and return it, single_turn ensures it doesn't accidentally start a conversation with the user, which would waste tokens and time. What happens to the conversation history when a sub-agent is in task mode? Answer: In ADK 2.0, task-mode agents operate in a "branch" of the session. While they have access to the relevant history to perform their task, the parent agent remains the "source of truth." When the task completes, the results are bubbled up to the parent's context. How does the mode setting improve the reliability of complex workflows? Answer: It makes the "Return to Parent" behavior deterministic. Instead of hoping the LLM will remember to hand back control, the framework enforces the return based on the mode. This prevents "lost in thought" scenarios where a sub-agent continues chatting with the user indefinitely instead of returning to the main workflow. Bonus Solution: weather_checker as an AgentTool​ from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.tools import google_search from google.adk.tools.agent_tool import AgentTool # No mode needed -- AgentTool doesn't use the sub_agents lifecycle at all. weather_agent = Agent( name="weather_checker", model="gemini-3.8-flash", tools=[google_search], instruction=( "Use google_search to look up current weather conditions and provide " "a brief, grounded 3-day weather forecast for the user's destination." ), ) flight_agent = Agent( name="flight_booker", model="gemini-3.8-flash", mode="task", rerun_on_resume=True, tools=[google_search], instruction=( "Help the user find a flight using google_search, ask for preferences if needed, " "confirm the simulated selection (no actual ticket purchase), and finish the task." ), ) root_agent = Agent( name="travel_planner", model="gemini-3.8-flash", rerun_on_resume=True, instruction=""" You are a travel planning coordinator. 1. Call the `weather_checker` tool to get the forecast. 2. Call the `flight_booker` to arrange travel. 3. Once both sub-tasks are done, present a final summary to the user. """, tools=[AgentTool(agent=weather_agent)], sub_agents=[flight_agent], ) Verified live: the result is the same forecast text, but the Trace tab shows no separate weather_checker author entry -- the call and its result appear as a single function call/response pair inside travel_planner's own turn, exactly like calling a regular tool.

documents.t: 🧭 Where We Are in Part 3: In Chapter A (Modules 15–16), Gemini decided dynamically which sub_agents to call. Welcome to Chapter B: Graph & Code Workflows (Modules 17–20)! Starting here, your graph controls the exact execution order — with zero LLM routing guesswork — using ADK 2.0's Workflow container and edges. Figure: Deterministic graph orchestration utilizing linear execution, concurrent fan-out, and join synchronization.
documents.s: Module 17: Static Workflows - Linear and Parallel Edges

documents.t: When a business process must always run in a predictable sequence or in parallel (for example: check warehouse inventory AND verify customer credit simultaneously, wait for both, then confirm the order), you don't want an LLM deciding whether to skip a step. Instead, you replace a standalone Agent as your root_agent with a Workflow graph made of three simple pieces: Nodes: Your individual Agent specialists (or synchronisation barriers). Edges: Directed tuples (source, target) defining the exact execution order. "START": The reserved entry point telling the Workflow which node(s) run first when a message arrives.

When you connect nodes in a chain, ADK executes them one after another: from google.adk import Workflow # START -> researcher -> writer -> editor my_pipeline = Workflow( name="SequentialSystem", edges=[ ("START", researcher), (researcher, writer), (writer, editor) ] ) Edge Shorthand: You can also write a multi-hop chain as a single tuple (A, B, C), which is shorthand for (A, B) followed by (B, C). For example, ("START", researcher, writer, editor) defines the exact same pipeline.

When multiple edges originate from the same source (such as "START" or an upstream node), ADK executes all target branches concurrently: # task_a and task_b run simultaneously parallel_run = Workflow( name="ParallelSystem", edges=[ ("START", task_a), ("START", task_b) ] )

Figure: Multi-stage workflow topology demonstrating concurrent branch execution converging into a barrier join node. When parallel branches finish, you often need to wait for all of them before running a final aggregation step. This pattern is called Fan-In, and it is handled by JoinNode. A JoinNode acts as a synchronization barrier: it pauses execution until every incoming edge has completed, and only then fires its outgoing edge. from google.adk import Workflow from google.adk.workflow import JoinNode syncer = JoinNode(name="sync_point") # Fan-out from START to task_a and task_b, converge at syncer, then run final_task complex_graph = Workflow( name="HybridSystem", edges=[ ("START", task_a, syncer), # Shorthand for ("START", task_a) + (task_a, syncer) ("START", task_b, syncer), # Shorthand for ("START", task_b) + (task_b, syncer) (syncer, final_task) ] )

When multiple parallel branches converge into a JoinNode, a single downstream agent needs a clean way to read both upstream results separately. ADK solves this using Session State Interpolation: Each upstream branch saves its output under a unique key using output_key (introduced in Module 04). The downstream agent references those saved keys directly inside its instruction string using curly braces {key_name}. weather_scout = Agent( name="weather_scout", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="Summarize the weekend weather forecast for the requested city.", output_key="weather_info", # Stored in session.state["weather_info"] ) events_scout = Agent( name="events_scout", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="List 3 popular cultural events happening this weekend in the city.", output_key="local_events", # Stored in session.state["local_events"] ) city_briefing = Agent( name="city_briefing", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="Create a short weekend guide combining WEATHER: {weather_info} and EVENTS: {local_events}.", ) Before sending the prompt to Gemini, ADK automatically replaces {weather_info} and {local_events} with the values stored in session.state.

Performance: Parallel execution reduces total latency to the duration of the slowest branch. Predictability: The path is fixed and code-defined; there is no risk of routing hallucinations. Transparency: The Dev UI Graph View gives you a 1:1 visual map of your business process. 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer In a parallel `Workflow` where two upstream branches converge into a `JoinNode`, how should a downstream summarizer agent cleanly access both upstream outputs? AEach upstream agent sets a distinct `output_key`, and the summarizer references them via `{key_name}` placeholders in its `instruction`BThe JoinNode automatically concatenates all agent names into a Python tupleCThe summarizer must re-run both upstream agents using `sub_agents`DParallel branches cannot share session state in ADK 2.0 Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

Edges define the flow: Chain nodes sequentially or fan them out from a shared source for parallel execution. JoinNode acts as the barrier synchronization point for parallel branches (Fan-In). output_key + {placeholder}: Upstream branches save named outputs to session state, and downstream agents inject them cleanly into their instruction templates.

In this lab, you will build a sophisticated News Aggregator using a hybrid graph architecture. You will learn how to: Run two specialized research nodes in parallel (Fan-out). Synchronize the results using a JoinNode (Fan-in). Process the combined data in a sequential step.
┌──── Node A (Tech News) ────┐ START ──┼ ├──→ JoinNode → Summarizer → END └──── Node B (Market News) ──┘

Exercise: Complete the root_agent definition using the edges parameter to implement the Fan-out/Join pattern. Tip: A 3-element edge tuple (A, B, C) is shorthand for two chained edges, A → B and B → C. So a parallel branch that both starts at "START" and converges on the syncer can be written as one tuple, ("START", tech_researcher, syncer), instead of two separate tuples. # 1. Create the synchronization point syncer = JoinNode(name="news_sync") # 2. Build the Workflow # TODO: Define the edges to: # - Start both researchers in parallel from "START". # - Converge both researchers at the 'syncer'. # - Connect the 'syncer' to the 'summarizer'. root_agent = Workflow( name="NewsSystem", edges=[ # Parallel Branch 1 ("START", ..., ...), # Parallel Branch 2 (..., ..., ...), # Sequential Final Step (..., ...) ] )

Return to the parent directory and start the Dev UI: cd .. uv run adk web (Select news_aggregator from the agent dropdown in the UI). Test: Send the prompt "Give me today's update." Inspect: Open the Graph View. Verify that the researchers start at the same time and the summarizer only runs after both finish. Known issue (upstream google-adk 2.8.0): the main static Graph View tab works fine for Workflow/JoinNode graphs like this one. However, clicking into an individual event's Graph inspector (the per-event highlight view in the Trace) currently throws a 500 error -- AttributeError: 'Workflow' object has no attribute '_graph' -- for this graph type specifically. This is an upstream ADK tooling bug, not something you did wrong. Workaround: use the main Graph View tab to inspect the overall structure instead of the per-event inspector.

You have built a hybrid multi-agent graph! You mastered Fan-out by defining multiple edges from START. You mastered Fan-in using the JoinNode. You learned that sequential and parallel execution are just different edge configurations. A few things worth internalizing: the JoinNode waits for every incoming edge -- if one parallel branch fails, it won't fire, so production graphs need retry/error handling to guarantee convergence.

What happens if one of the parallel researchers fails? Can you add a third researcher (e.g., 'sports_researcher') to this hybrid graph? What single line would you add? Why use output_key here if ADK 2.0 already passes data between sequential nodes automatically?

Record this lab as completed in your study plan? ✓ Mark as Complete Lab 17 Solution: Building a Hybrid News Aggregator Goal​ This file contains the complete code for the agent.py script using the ADK 2.0 Hybrid Graph pattern (Sequential + Parallel). news_aggregator/agent.py​ from google.adk import Agent, Workflow from google.adk.workflow import JoinNode # 1. Define Specialist Nodes tech_researcher = Agent( name="tech_researcher", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="Find 3 exciting headlines about AI and Robotics. Be concise.", output_key="tech_news" ) market_researcher = Agent( name="market_researcher", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="Find 3 key headlines about Stock Market trends. Be concise.", output_key="market_news" ) summarizer = Agent( name="summarizer", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction=""" You are a news editor. Create a brief newsletter using the data provided: TECH: {tech_news} MARKET: {market_news} Synthesize the information into a single, cohesive daily briefing. """ ) # 2. Define the Synchronization Point syncer = JoinNode(name="news_sync") # 3. Assemble the Workflow # Parallel Fan-out + Sequential Fan-in root_agent = Workflow( name="NewsSystem", edges=[ # Both start at the same time and connect to the same JoinNode ("START", tech_researcher, syncer), ("START", market_researcher, syncer), # Once both are done, the syncer triggers the summarizer (syncer, summarizer) ] ) Self-Reflection Answers​ What happens if one of the parallel researchers fails? Answer: By default, the JoinNode waits for ALL incoming edges. If one fails, the JoinNode will not fire its outgoing edge, potentially stalling the workflow. In production, you would add retry logic or error handling to ensure the graph can still converge. Can I add a third researcher (e.g., 'sports_researcher')? Answer: Yes! You just define the agent and add a third edge: ("START", sports_researcher, syncer). The syncer will automatically wait for all three. Why use output_key if data flows automatically? Answer: While ADK 2.0 passes the output of one node to the next, a JoinNode receives multiple outputs. Using output_key saves individual results into the global session state, making it much easier for the summarizer to access specific variables like {tech_news} via string interpolation.

documents.t: Static edges (Module 17) are unbeatable when every step in your pipeline is fixed ahead of time. When execution depends on runtime conditions, Dynamic Workflows let you write an ordinary Python async def function that calls agents just like regular Python functions!

Figure: Programmatic node invocation lifecycle with context state inspection, adaptive node dispatch, and result aggregation. ADK 2.0 introduces two simple primitives for programmable orchestration: @node (from google.adk.workflow): A decorator that turns any Python function into a graph node that a Workflow can run. await ctx.run_node(target_node, input_data): Executes an Agent (or another node) and returns its output directly into a Python variable! from google.adk import Agent, Workflow, Context from google.adk.workflow import node # 1. Define specialist agents as usual # IMPORTANT: Every child Agent invoked dynamically via ctx.run_node() inside # a @node(rerun_on_resume=True) orchestrator MUST also set rerun_on_resume=True! researcher = Agent( name="researcher", model="gemini-3.8-flash", rerun_on_resume=True, instruction="Research key facts about the user's topic.", ) writer = Agent( name="writer", model="gemini-3.8-flash", rerun_on_resume=True, instruction="Turn the provided research notes into a short, engaging article.", ) # 2. Write a Python orchestrator decorated with @node @node(rerun_on_resume=True) async def newsletter_workflow(ctx: Context, node_input: str): # Step A: Run researcher and store its answer in a normal Python variable research_notes = await ctx.run_node(researcher, node_input) # Step B: Use standard Python if/else or string formatting freely! if len(research_notes) < 50: return "Not enough public information found on this topic." # Step C: Pass research_notes directly into writer and return its final article final_article = await ctx.run_node(writer, research_notes) return final_article # 3. Register the orchestrator as the Workflow's entry point root_agent = Workflow( name="NewsletterSystem", edges=[("START", newsletter_workflow)], ) Line-by-Line Breakdown of the New Primitives​ @node(rerun_on_resume=True) & Child Agent(..., rerun_on_resume=True): Registers newsletter_workflow as a workflow node. In ADK 2.0, both the @node(rerun_on_resume=True) orchestrator and every child Agent invoked dynamically via await ctx.run_node(child, ...) must set rerun_on_resume=True so multi-turn conversations re-execute cleanly on subsequent user messages without raising ValueError: A node must have rerun_on_resume=True. async def newsletter_workflow(ctx: Context, node_input: str):: ctx: Context is ADK's runtime control object (giving you ctx.run_node(...) and ctx.session.state). node_input: str is the incoming user message (because "START" connects to this function). await ctx.run_node(researcher, node_input): Runs researcher with node_input as its prompt and returns the result directly: If the agent returns plain text, you get a str. If the agent has a Pydantic output_schema, ADK automatically parses the JSON and returns a plain Python dict (e.g., result["approved"]). return final_article: Whatever your @node function returns is emitted as the workflow's final response to the user!

Multi-Step Conditional Chains: Run Agent A, inspect or combine its result in Python, and conditionally pass enriched context to Agent B. Direct Variable Passing: No need for output_key or {placeholder} templates — outputs live in normal Python variables. Full Trace Visibility: Even though routing happens in Python, ADK's Workflow Runtime still records every ctx.run_node() call in the Dev UI Trace tab!

Because every @node function is a first-class ADK component, you can also pass a @node directly into an Agent's tools=[...] list without any extra wrapper: from google.adk import Agent, Context from google.adk.workflow import node @node async def calculate_vip_discount(ctx: Context, tier: str) -> str: """Calculates the discount rate for a given customer tier.""" return "20% VIP discount" if "VIP" in tier.upper() else "5% standard discount" root_agent = Agent( model="gemini-3.8-flash", name="pricing_agent", instruction="Help customers with discounts using the calculate_vip_discount tool.", tools=[calculate_vip_discount], ) 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer When `await ctx.run_node(topic_checker, node_input)` executes an `Agent` configured with a Pydantic `output_schema`, what Python type does `run_node()` return at runtime? AA raw unparsed XML stringBA plain Python `dict` matching the schema fields (accessed via `result['field']`)CAn unawaited coroutine objectDNone — results can only be read from disk Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

documents.t: @node(rerun_on_resume=True) turns a standard async def Python function into a programmable workflow orchestrator. await ctx.run_node(node, input) executes any agent and returns its output directly (str, or dict when output_schema is set). Use Module 17 for fixed pipelines, and Module 18 when orchestration requires conditional multi-step Python logic!

In this lab, you will build a conditional multi-step orchestration system using a Dynamic Workflow — doing something Module 17's fixed static edges cannot do: Run classifier to detect the customer's sentiment ("angry", "neutral", or "happy"). If the customer is not angry, simply call ai_support and return its technical answer. If the customer is "angry", execute a dynamic 2-step chain: First, call ai_support to draft a quick technical troubleshooting note. Second, pass both the customer's original message and that technical draft into human_escalation, so the escalation team responds with empathy and an immediate technical fix! This shows the real superpower of @node + ctx.run_node(): chaining and combining multiple agent outputs in plain Python variables.

Specialist Agent Nodes ===== # Every child Agent invoked via ctx.run_node() inside @node(rerun_on_resume=True) # must also set rerun_on_resume=True so multi-turn sessions re-run cleanly. ai_support = Agent( name="ai_support_bot", model="gemini-3.8-flash", rerun_on_resume=True, instruction="You are a helpful customer support AI. Answer technical questions clearly.", ) human_escalation = Agent( name="human_escalation_team", model="gemini-3.8-flash", rerun_on_resume=True, instruction=( "You are a senior human escalation rep handling a frustrated customer. " "Apologize sincerely, promise a follow-up call, and include any preliminary " "technical troubleshooting steps provided to you." ), ) # ===== 2. Classifier Agent Node ===== class SentimentClassification(BaseModel): sentiment: Literal["angry", "neutral", "happy"] classifier = Agent( name="classifier", model="gemini-3.8-flash", rerun_on_resume=True, instruction="Classify the sentiment of the user's latest message.", output_schema=SentimentClassification, ) # ===== 3. Build the Dynamic Workflow (The Orchestrator) ===== @node(rerun_on_resume=True) async def support_router_workflow(ctx: Context, node_input: str): # Step 3a: Run the classifier node. # run_node() returns the structured output directly as a plain Python dict. classification: dict = await ctx.run_node(classifier, node_input) # Step 3b: Dynamic multi-step orchestration using plain Python control flow. if classification["sentiment"] == "angry": # Chain 2 agents dynamically: first draft a technical fix, then escalate with context! tech_draft = await ctx.run_node(ai_support, node_input) escalation_prompt = ( f"Customer message: {node_input}\n\n" f"Preliminary technical analysis: {tech_draft}" ) return await ctx.run_node(human_escalation, escalation_prompt) # Standard path: single call to AI support return await ctx.run_node(ai_support, node_input) # ===== 4. Register the Workflow as the Root ===== root_agent = Workflow( name="SupportSystem", edges=[("START", support_router_workflow)] ) Self-Reflection Answers​ How does passing data with ctx.run_node() in a Dynamic Workflow differ from passing data with output_key in Static Edges (Module 17)? Answer: With Static Edges (Module 17), you save results into session.state via output_key and reference them via {placeholders} inside static instruction strings. In a Dynamic Workflow, ctx.run_node() returns the agent's output directly into a normal Python variable (a string, or a plain dict when using output_schema), so you can inspect, combine, or transform outputs in pure Python before passing them to the next node. Why is it important to set rerun_on_resume=True for the orchestrator node (and its dynamically invoked child agents)? Answer: Dynamic workflows are resumable across conversational turns. In ADK 2.0, setting rerun_on_resume=True on both the @node orchestrator and every child Agent called via await ctx.run_node(...) ensures that on subsequent user turns in the same session, both the orchestrator and its specialist sub-nodes re-execute cleanly instead of raising ValueError: A node must have rerun_on_resume=True. Can a dynamic workflow call another dynamic workflow? Answer: Yes! In ADK 2.0, every Workflow and every @node function is just a Node. This allows for deep nesting and modularity: you can build complex systems by composing many small, testable dynamic workflows together.
