Here is the official reference walkthrough and architecture review: 🎉 Challenge Lab Unlocked! Record this lab as completed in your study plan? ✓ Mark as Complete Lab 22 Solution: Building a Personal Learning Tutor​ Goal​ This solution provides the complete implementation for the Personal Learning Tutor (personal_tutor/agent.py), the SQLite multi-session persistence & memory archive script (personal_tutor/test_session_persistence.py), and the optional context compaction & rewind script (personal_tutor/test_memory_advanced.py). personal_tutor/agent.py​ """ Personal Learning Tutor - Demonstrates Session State & Memory Management This agent uses: - user: prefix for persistent preferences (language, difficulty) - Session state (unprefixed) for current topic tracking - app: prefix for global catalog metadata ({app:course_version?}) - temp: prefix for single-turn quiz calculations - Simulated long-term memory search across past lessons """ from datetime import datetime, timezone from pathlib import Path from typing import Any, Dict from dotenv import load_dotenv from google.adk.agents import Agent from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext # Load local .env if present (override=True helps override stale shell vars during local labs) load_dotenv(Path(__file__).with_name(".env"), override=True) ALLOWED_DIFFICULTIES = {"beginner", "intermediate", "advanced"} # ============================================================================ # TOOLS: State Management & Memory Operations # ============================================================================ def set_user_preferences( language: str, difficulty_level: str, tool_context: ToolContext, ) -> Dict[str, Any]: """ Set user learning preferences (stored persistently across all sessions). Args: language: Preferred language code or name (en, es, fr, it, etc.) difficulty_level: beginner, intermediate, or advanced """ clean_lang = language.strip()[:20] or "en" norm_diff = difficulty_level.strip().lower() if norm_diff not in ALLOWED_DIFFICULTIES: norm_diff = "beginner" tool_context.state["user:language"] = clean_lang tool_context.state["user:difficulty_level"] = norm_diff return { "status": "success", "message": f"Preferences saved: {clean_lang}, {norm_diff} level", } def record_topic_completion( topic: str, quiz_score: int, tool_context: ToolContext, ) -> Dict[str, Any]: """ Record that the user completed a topic (stored persistently across sessions). Args: topic: Topic name (e.g., "Python Basics", "Data Structures") quiz_score: Score out of 100 """ topics = list(tool_context.state.get("user:topics_covered", [])) scores = dict(tool_context.state.get("user:quiz_scores", {})) if topic not in topics: topics.append(topic) scores[topic] = quiz_score tool_context.state["user:topics_covered"] = topics tool_context.state["user:quiz_scores"] = scores return { "status": "success", "topics_count": len(topics), "message": f"Recorded: {topic} with score {quiz_score}/100", } def get_user_progress(tool_context: ToolContext) -> Dict[str, Any]: """ Get the user's learning progress summary across all sessions. """ language = tool_context.state.get("user:language", "en") difficulty = tool_context.state.get("user:difficulty_level", "beginner") topics = list(tool_context.state.get("user:topics_covered", [])) scores = dict(tool_context.state.get("user:quiz_scores", {})) avg_score = sum(scores.values()) / len(scores) if scores else 0.0 return { "status": "success", "language": language, "difficulty_level": difficulty, "topics_completed": len(topics), "topics": topics, "average_quiz_score": round(avg_score, 1), "all_scores": scores, } def start_learning_session( topic: str, tool_context: ToolContext, ) -> Dict[str, Any]: """ Start a new learning session for a topic. Uses unprefixed session state to track the active topic in this session only. """ tool_context.state["current_topic"] = topic tool_context.state["session_start_time"] = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat() difficulty = tool_context.state.get("user:difficulty_level", "beginner") return { "status": "success", "topic": topic, "difficulty_level": difficulty, "message": f"Started learning session: {topic} at {difficulty} level", } def calculate_quiz_grade( correct_answers: int, total_questions: int, tool_context: ToolContext, ) -> Dict[str, Any]: """ Calculate a quiz grade using temporary invocation-scoped state (temp:). DatabaseSessionService (google-adk[db]) uses SQLAlchemy 2.0's async engine: sqlite+aiosqlite:/// is great for single-instance local/CI testing, while postgresql+asyncpg:// (Cloud SQL / AlloyDB) unlocks row-level SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locking for multi-replica Cloud Run / GKE deployments. Why is temp: state automatically discarded after each turn, and why must secrets still never be placed in temp:? Answer: temp: state is scoped strictly to the current invocation_id for transient scratchpad calculations, preventing database bloat and state pollution across turns. However, temp: deltas are still emitted inside live Event streams and observability traces—so API keys and OAuth tokens belong in Secret Manager or ADK AuthCredential stores, never session.state. Answer: session.state (including user: and app: prefixes) excels at structured key-value attributes looked up by exact key name (user:language, current_topic). MemoryService (add_session_to_memory / search_memory) archives unstructured knowledge across past conversations so an agent can recall open-ended discussions weeks later without keeping every historical event inside the active context window. When runner.rewind_async(...) rolls back a turn, why does user: state remain untouched? Answer: Rewind restores session-scoped state and session artifacts to their snapshot prior to rewind_before_invocation_id (resetting keys introduced after that point to None), undoing conversational missteps in the current thread without erasing global app: settings or durable user: profile preferences shared across other sessions.

Agents often need to create and persist files (reports, data, images) that live beyond a single conversation. Simple state is not enough for this; you need a proper file management system. The ADK provides this through Artifacts. Artifacts provide structured file storage with powerful features that are critical for production agents: 💾 Persistence: Files survive across agent sessions. 📝 Versioning: Every time a file is saved, a new version is created automatically, providing a complete history. 🔍 Discoverability: Agents can list and search for all available artifacts. 📊 Audit Trail: The version history allows you to track who created what and when. 🔐 Credentials: A related system provides secure storage for secrets like API keys.

An artifact is a versioned file stored by the agent system. Each save operation creates a new, immutable version, and all previous versions are retained. Figure: Artifact versioning lifecycle and immutable storage pipeline across session boundaries. Important: Artifact versions are 0-indexed. The first save of a file creates version 0.

Before using artifacts, you must configure an artifact_service in your Runner. InMemoryArtifactService: Stores artifacts in volatile RAM (lost on process exit). Ideal for fast unit tests and InMemoryRunner. FileArtifactService: Stores versioned artifacts on the local filesystem (file://<path>). Used automatically by uv run adk web (<agent>/.adk/artifacts/) unless --no_use_local_storage is passed! GcsArtifactService: The cloud production solution (gs://<bucket>). Stores versioned artifacts durably in a Google Cloud Storage bucket across multi-replica deployments. # Local volatile testing from google.adk.artifacts import InMemoryArtifactService, FileArtifactService, GcsArtifactService from google.adk.runners import Runner artifact_service = InMemoryArtifactService() # Local filesystem persistence local_artifact_service = FileArtifactService(root_dir="./local_artifacts") # Production Google Cloud Storage gcs_artifact_service = GcsArtifactService(bucket_name="your-gcs-bucket") # Attach to Runner runner = Runner( app_name="doc_app", agent=root_agent, session_service=session_service, artifact_service=gcs_artifact_service, )

The primary way to work with artifacts is from within an asynchronous custom tool using the ToolContext. All artifact operations are async and must be awaited. await tool_context.save_artifact(filename, artifact): Saves a types.Part object as a new version of a file and returns the new version number. await tool_context.load_artifact(filename, version=None): Loads the content of an artifact. If version is omitted, it loads the latest version. await tool_context.list_artifacts(): Returns a list of all artifact filenames available in the current session.
documents.s: How Agents and Tools Interact with Artifacts

documents.t: One of the main reasons to use Artifacts instead of simple state is to handle binary data. While text uses types.Part.from_text(), binary files use types.Part.from_bytes(). You must always specify the MIME type (e.g., image/png, application/pdf) so the system knows how to handle the file. # Saving an image inside an async tool image_data = b'\x89PNG\r\n...' # Raw bytes part = types.Part.from_bytes(data=image_data, mime_type='image/png') await tool_context.save_artifact('chart.png', part)

By default, artifacts are scoped to the current session. When the session ends, they are no longer accessible to the agent (though they may still exist in storage). To make an artifact persistent for a specific user across multiple sessions, prefix the filename with user:. "report.txt" -> Visible only in the current conversation. "user:preferences.json" -> Visible to this user in any conversation they start.

Never store sensitive API keys or OAuth tokens in session.state (user: or app:) or unencrypted artifacts. Instead, ADK provides a dedicated credential subsystem for runtime secrets and user-delegated OAuth tokens: await tool_context.save_credential(auth_config) await tool_context.load_credential(auth_config) This subsystem pairs an AuthConfig object with a CredentialService (or Google Cloud Secret Manager for service-level keys) so sensitive tokens stay isolated from conversation logs, trace exports, and cross-user state tables. Going Further: this module's lab doesn't exercise Credential Management hands-on — setting up a real OAuth flow is more infrastructure than a single lab warrants. If you want to try it, wire up save_credential/load_credential around a real third-party OAuth provider and confirm a tool can use the stored token on a later call, in a later session. 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer In Google ADK, what version number is assigned the first time you call await tool_context.save_artifact('user:report.pdf', part), and how is that file scoped? AVersion 0, accessible across all future sessions belonging to the same userBVersion 1, restricted strictly to the current turn and deleted afterwardCVersion 0, shared globally across every user of the applicationDVersion 1, stored directly inside the session.state JSON dictionary Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

The ADK's Artifacts system provides persistent, versioned file storage for agents. Binary Support: Unlike simple text memory, Artifacts handle images, PDFs, and audio using types.Part.from_bytes(). Scoping: Use the user: prefix (e.g., user:settings.json) to persist files across multiple sessions for the same user. Versioning and Auditability: Automatic 0-indexed versioning provides an immutable audit trail, allowing you to trace changes and inspect prior file revisions. Pluggable Storage Backends: adk web uses FileArtifactService (.adk/artifacts/) locally by default; unit tests use InMemoryArtifactService, and cloud deployments use GcsArtifactService. Tools interact with artifacts asynchronously using ToolContext (save_artifact, load_artifact, list_artifacts). Asynchronous Operations: All interactions with the Artifact Service are asynchronous (async/await) so file and cloud storage I/O never blocks the Python event loop.

In this lab, you will build a Document Processor agent (doc_processor) that reads a real source document (either from a local doc_processor/sample_docs/ folder or uploaded directly inside the adk web chat) and processes it through a 4-stage pipeline, saving the output of every stage as an immutable, versioned ADK Artifact.

Extract & Clean Text (extract_text): Sanitizes the document name, reads the real .txt source file (from doc_processor/sample_docs/ or a chat file attachment), normalizes messy whitespace/blank lines, and saves {clean_name}_extracted.txt as an artifact. Summarize (summarize_document): Loads {clean_name}_extracted.txt from the Artifact Service, extracts real word counts, headline context, and financial/operational metrics from the text, and saves {clean_name}_summary.txt. Generate Chart (generate_chart): Verifies {clean_name}_extracted.txt exists, computes real character/word/numeric-figure statistics from the extracted text, and saves a binary PNG (image/png) artifact as {clean_name}_chart.png. Compile Audit Report (create_report): Queries list_artifacts(), verifies the exact expected artifacts exist in presentation order (_summary.txt → _chart.png → _extracted.txt), and compiles them into {clean_name}_FINAL_REPORT.md.

documents.t: Verify your credentials in doc_processor/.env (or in your workspace .env). From your adk-training workspace directory, start the Dev UI: uv run adk web Note on Local vs. Cloud Persistence: doc_processor reads input .txt files from doc_processor/sample_docs/ (or from chat file attachments) and saves versioned output artifacts locally inside doc_processor/.adk/artifacts/ via FileArtifactService (--use_local_storage default). Pass --no_use_local_storage for volatile RAM testing, or --artifact_service_uri="gs://your-bucket" (GcsArtifactService) in multi-replica cloud deployments. Select doc_processor in the top-left agent dropdown and walk through these 3 verification scenarios: 3.1 Happy Path — Real Extraction, Metrics Summary & Audit Report (version 0): If you chose Option A (sample_docs/): send: Process the document named 'Annual_Report_2025'. If you chose Option B (Chat Upload): click More options (+) → Upload local file in the bottom chat bar, attach Annual_Report_2025.txt, and send: Process 'Annual_Report_2025'. Open the Artifacts tab/panel in adk web: inspect Annual_Report_2025_extracted.txt, Annual_Report_2025_summary.txt, Annual_Report_2025_chart.png, and Annual_Report_2025_FINAL_REPORT.md (version 0). Confirm that the extra spaces were cleaned and that the real $48.6M / $52.1M ARR metrics from the file appear inside the summary and final report! 3.2 Auditability & Versioning (version 0 → version 1): Open doc_processor/sample_docs/Annual_Report_2025.txt in your editor (or edit your local copy if using Option B), change Total Revenue: $48.6M to Total Revenue: $51.2M (Audited), and save the file. Send the prompt again in the same session (Option B users: re-attach your updated Annual_Report_2025.txt via More options (+) → Upload local file along with the prompt): Process the document named 'Annual_Report_2025' again with the updated figures. Notice that every artifact advances to version 1 while version 0 remains preserved in the Artifact history for side-by-side audit comparison! (Bonus: create a second file like doc_processor/sample_docs/Q1_Notes.txt and process it too!) 3.3 Guided Missing-File Error Handling: Test what happens when a requested file does not exist: Process 'Missing_File'. Verify that extract_text stops cleanly without crashing, lists the valid files available inside doc_processor/sample_docs/ (such as Annual_Report_2025.txt, or none if you only used Option B chat uploads), and prevents downstream tools from running on empty data.

You have built an end-to-end, auditable document processing agent backed by real file input and ADK Artifacts: Sanitized user-supplied document names against path traversal and loaded real .txt inputs from doc_processor/sample_docs/ or adk web chat attachments (tool_context.user_content). Saved binary PNG artifacts with types.Part.from_bytes(..., mime_type="image/png") and compiled expected artifacts in deterministic order without prefix collisions. Verified immutable 0-indexed artifact versioning (version 0 → version 1) when re-processing modified source files.

Why is this a requirement for functions that interact with the Artifact Service? Locally, uv run adk web uses FileArtifactService (.adk/artifacts/). """, tools=[ FunctionTool(extract_text), FunctionTool(summarize_document), FunctionTool(generate_chart), FunctionTool(create_report), ], ) Self-Reflection Answers​ Why is the versioning feature of the Artifacts system important for auditability and debugging in a production environment? Answer: Versioning is crucial because it provides an immutable history of every file generated or modified by the agent. When you edited Annual_Report_2025.txt and re-ran the pipeline, ADK preserved version 0 alongside version 1. For auditability, you can prove exactly which source snapshot produced a given executive report; for debugging, you can compare intermediate artifacts across versions to pinpoint regressions. All the tool functions in this lab are async. Why is this a requirement for functions that interact with the Artifact Service? Answer: Interacting with file storage (especially cloud object stores like Google Cloud Storage) involves network I/O operations that can take tens or hundreds of milliseconds. Using async def with await ensures I/O-bound tasks never block the Python event loop, keeping the agent server responsive under concurrent requests. Locally, uv run adk web uses FileArtifactService (.adk/artifacts/). How do you configure GcsArtifactService for multi-replica cloud production? In traditional software development, we rely on unit tests and integration tests to ensure our code is correct. These tests check for specific, predictable outcomes. For example, assert add(2, 2) == 4. This works because the add function is deterministic—it will always produce the same output for the same input. However, Agents are non-deterministic. Due to the probabilistic nature of Large Language Models, asking the same question twice might yield slightly different, yet equally correct, answers. User: "What's the weather in Paris?" Acceptable Answer 1: "The weather in Paris is currently sunny and 22°C." Acceptable Answer 2: "It's a sunny day in Paris, with a temperature of 22 degrees Celsius." A simple string comparison would fail for the second answer, even though it's perfectly valid. This variability means we need a more sophisticated way to evaluate our agents.

Agent evaluation is less about "pass/fail" and more about measuring quality and correctness. The ADK's evaluation framework is built on comparing an agent's actual behavior against a "golden" or "reference" example that you provide. Figure: Golden dataset evaluation pipeline and LLM-as-a-judge trajectory benchmarking matrix. This evaluation can be broken down into two key areas: 1. Evaluating the Final Response​ This assesses the quality of the agent's final answer to the user. Instead of an exact match, we can use more flexible criteria: Semantic Similarity: Does the agent's response mean the same thing as the reference response? This can be judged by another LLM. Rubrics: Does the response meet certain quality criteria? (e.g., "Is the tone helpful?", "Is the answer concise?"). Groundedness: Does the agent's answer contain any "hallucinations" (facts that it made up), or is it properly grounded in the information it received from its tools? 2. Evaluating the Trajectory​ This is unique to agents and is often more important than the final response. The trajectory is the sequence of steps the agent took to arrive at its answer. This includes which tools it called, in what order, and with what arguments. By evaluating the trajectory, you are testing the agent's reasoning process. Did it use the right tool for the job? Did it call its tools in the correct sequence? For example, if a user asks to book a flight and then a hotel, the expected trajectory might be: Call search_flights tool. Call book_flight tool. Call search_hotels tool. Call book_hotel tool. If the agent tries to book the hotel before searching for flights, its trajectory is incorrect, even if it eventually produces a valid booking. The ADK's evaluation tools allow you to perform an exact match on the tool trajectory, ensuring your agent follows the correct process every time.

The ADK evaluation workflow revolves around creating Evaluation Cases. An evaluation case is a recording of a conversation, including: The user's messages. The expected final response from the agent. The expected intermediate tool calls (the trajectory). You can create these evaluation cases manually in a JSON file, but the easiest way is to use the ADK Developer UI. You can have a conversation with your agent, and if you're satisfied with the outcome, you can save that entire conversation as a new evaluation case with a single click. Once you have a set of evaluation cases, you can run them automatically: From the Dev UI, to get a quick visual report. From the command line (uv run adk eval), for automated checks. Programmatically (using pytest), to integrate agent evaluation into your CI/CD pipeline. By building a suite of evaluation cases, you create a safety net. Every time you change your agent's instructions or tools, you can re-run your evaluations to ensure you haven't caused a regression in its behavior. This brings the reliability of traditional software testing to the non-deterministic world of AI agents.
documents.s: How Evaluation Works in the ADK

documents.t: The Testing Pyramid​ A robust testing strategy for AI agents involves multiple layers, often visualized as a pyramid. This approach, adapted from traditional software engineering, ensures you have a fast and reliable feedback loop. ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════╗ ║ EVALUATION TESTS ║ ║ (End-to-End Quality, LLM-in-the-loop) ║ ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════╝ │ │ Slowest, most realistic, checks overall quality ▼ ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════╗ ║ INTEGRATION TESTS ║ ║ (Agent logic, tool orchestration) ║ ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════╝ │ │ Medium speed, validates system interactions ▼ ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════╗ ║ UNIT TESTS ║ ║ (Tool functions, deterministic logic) ║ ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════╝ Unit Tests (Base): These are fast, deterministic tests for the smallest parts of your agent, primarily your custom tool functions. You test them with pytest just like any other Python code, mocking any external dependencies. The vast majority of your tests should be here. Integration Tests (Middle): These tests verify that the components of your agent work together. For example, does your agent correctly call a sequence of tools? These tests often involve running the agent but mocking the final LLM call to keep them deterministic. Evaluation Tests (Top): This is the layer you've been learning about. These are end-to-end tests that involve the real LLM. They are the most realistic but also the slowest and non-deterministic. You use them to validate the overall quality of the agent's reasoning and final responses. Available Evaluation Metrics​ The ADK provides a comprehensive set of built-in metrics, categorized by what they assess: 1. Tool Use Trajectory (Reasoning) tool_trajectory_avg_score: Measures the accuracy of the agent's tool call sequence against an expected list. It supports EXACT, IN_ORDER, or ANY_ORDER matching. This is critical for regression testing workflows. rubric_based_tool_use_quality_v1: Uses an LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate tool usage against a custom rubric (e.g., "Did the agent select the most efficient tool?"). 2. Final Response Quality (Accuracy & Style) response_match_score (ROUGE): Measures n-gram overlap. Good for checking if key keywords are present. final_response_match_v2: Uses an LLM to check for semantic equivalence. Allows for different phrasing as long as the meaning is the same as the reference. rubric_based_final_response_quality_v1: Rates the response against subjective criteria you define (e.g., "politeness", "conciseness") using an LLM judge. 3. Groundedness and Safety (Compliance) hallucinations_v1: Checks if the response contains claims unsupported by the context (tool outputs). Essential for preventing misinformation. safety_v1: Evaluates the response for harmful content, ensuring compliance with safety guidelines.

Static test cases (like the "Golden Path" above) are excellent for regression testing—ensuring yesterday's features still work today. However, they can't test how your agent handles the unpredictable nature of real users. For this, the ADK provides User Simulation. Dynamic Prompt Generation: Instead of hard-coding user questions, you configure a ConversationScenario. Conversation Scenarios: You define a starting_prompt (e.g., "I want to buy a car") and a conversation_plan (e.g., "The user is budget-conscious and indecisive"). The Simulator: An LLM acts as the "User," generating dynamic responses based on your plan and the agent's replies. This allows you to "stress test" your agent against hundreds of diverse, generated conversations to find edge cases you might have missed manually. Note that for dynamic scenarios, you typically use reference-free metrics like safety_v1 and hallucinations_v1 since there is no single "expected" response.

🔭 Enterprise Preview (Covered in Depth in Part 6): In Lab 24, you will run evaluations directly with ADK's built-in Dev UI and uv run adk eval—no extra manifest files required! Below is an architectural preview of google-agents-cli (uvx google-agents-cli ... and agents-cli-manifest.yaml), the enterprise CI/CD and deployment companion covered in full detail in Part 6 (Deployment & Enterprise AgentOps), so you can see how your .evalset.json habits scale into production pipelines. In modern enterprise agent engineering, evaluation is not an isolated one-time test; it forms a continuous loop known as the Quality Flywheel: Automated Evaluation with agents-cli eval run​ While adk eval runs evaluations against .evalset.json files generated in the Dev UI, the official Google Agents CLI (google-agents-cli) provides an integrated evaluation runner designed for modern CI/CD pipelines and interactive benchmarking: Note: Like other agents-cli lifecycle commands, eval run expects an agents-cli-manifest.yaml in your project root (generated via uvx google-agents-cli scaffold enhance . or agents-cli create). # Run evaluation across all configured evaluation sets in the project uvx google-agents-cli eval run # Run evaluation targeting a specific evaluation dataset uvx google-agents-cli eval run --dataset tests/eval_datasets/golden_cases.json Evaluating Evaluation Datasets & Multi-Turn Schema​ An evaluation dataset defines the benchmark scenarios, expected tool calls, and reference outcomes. Below is the standard schema for evaluation cases: [ { "eval_case_id": "calculator_add_basic", "conversation": [ { "role": "user", "parts": [{ "text": "What is 10 + 5?" }] }, { "role": "model", "intermediate_tool_calls": [ { "name": "add", "args": { "a": 10, "b": 5 } } ], "parts": [{ "text": "The result of 10 + 5 is 15." }] } ], "metrics": { "tool_trajectory_avg_score": { "threshold": 1.0, "match_type": "EXACT" }, "final_response_match_v2": { "threshold": 0.85 } } } ] agents-cli eval vs adk eval Comparison​ Feature adk eval agents-cli eval run Primary Focus Local ADK framework unit/integration evaluation Enterprise AgentOps lifecycle & Quality Flywheel gate Dataset Source Local .evalset.json files from ADK Dev UI Project-level eval datasets and multi-scenario matrices Execution Engine Local ADK Python evaluation runner Multi-agent benchmarking engine with structured summary reports CI/CD Integration Direct pytest or CLI invocation Native exit-code quality gating for GitHub Actions / Cloud Build 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer Why is tool_trajectory_avg_score evaluation often prioritized over simple string response matching when regression testing complex ADK agents in CI/CD? ABecause validating the exact sequence of reasoning and tool invocations proves the agent followed the deterministic business workflow, regardless of semantic phrasing changes in the final textBBecause LLMs cannot output string responses in headless CI environmentsCBecause evaluating tool trajectories uses 0 API tokensDBecause tool calls cannot be recorded in evaluation datasets Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

documents.t: Agents are non-deterministic, so traditional pass/fail tests are insufficient. The ADK evaluation framework measures quality by comparing an agent's behavior against a recorded "golden path" or Evaluation Case. Metrics Categories: Evaluation covers Trajectory (did it follow the right steps?), Response Quality (is the answer correct/good?), and Safety/Groundedness (is it harmless and factual?). User Simulation: Use dynamic user simulation to test your agent against varied, LLM-generated personas and scenarios, going beyond static examples. Importance of Trajectory Testing: Testing the tool_trajectory is often more critical than just the final response because it validates the agent's underlying reasoning process. Continuous Quality Flywheel: Use uvx google-agents-cli eval run in your CI/CD pipelines to benchmark golden datasets before cloud deployment.

In this lab, you will learn the fundamental workflow of the ADK's evaluation feature. You will use the ADK Developer UI to have a "golden path" conversation with the Calculator agent (calculator_agent), save that conversation as an evaluation case, and re-run it from both the UI and CLI to validate the agent's behavior.

First, we need to have a conversation with the agent that represents the exact behavior we want to test. Open the Dev UI in your browser. Have the following, precise conversation: User: "What is 10 + 5?" Wait for the agent to respond. It should say something like: "The result of 10 + 5 is 15." This single-turn conversation will be our test case. We will test both the tool call (add(a=10, b=5)) and the final text response.

Now, let's save this conversation as a reusable test. Navigate to the "Eval" Tab: In the right-hand panel of the Dev UI, click on the "Eval" tab. Create a New Eval Set: An "Eval Set" is a collection of test cases. Click the "New Eval Set" button. Give it a name, for example, calculator_tests, and click "Create". Add the Session to the Eval Set: With your calculator_tests set selected, click the button that says "Add current session to eval set". You will be prompted for an "Eval Case ID". Give it a descriptive name like addition_test. Click "Save". Inspect the Saved Case: You will now see addition_test in the list of evaluation cases. Click on it. The UI will show you the recorded conversation, including the user message, the expected tool calls, and the expected final response. This is the "golden path" that future test runs will be compared against. Behind the scenes, the Dev UI has created a file at calculator_tests.evalset.json, directly inside your agent's directory — there is no separate eval_results/ folder.

Now that we have a saved test case, we can run it to validate the agent's behavior. Select the Test Case: In the "Eval" tab, make sure the checkbox next to addition_test is checked. Run the Evaluation: Click the "Run Evaluation" button. A dialog will appear allowing you to set the evaluation criteria. For this lab, the defaults are fine: tool_trajectory_avg_score: 1.0 (requires a perfect match of the tool calls) response_match_score: 0.8 (requires a high degree of similarity for the text response) Click "Start". Analyze the Results: The evaluation will run. This involves the ADK running the user message ("What is 10 + 5?") through the agent again and capturing the new results. You should see a "Pass" result appear in the "Evaluation History". Click on the "Pass" result to see the details. It will show you that the tool_trajectory_score was 1.0 (a perfect match) and the response_match_score was also 1.0 for this run. Note: LLMs aren't perfectly deterministic. If you re-run this eval later, don't be surprised if response_match_score comes back slightly below 1.0 (e.g. the agent says "The sum of 10 and 5 is 15." instead of the recorded "The result of 10 + 5 is 15."). As long as the score stays above the 0.8 threshold, the case still passes — see the Self-Reflection Questions for why this fuzzy matching exists.

Let's see what a failure looks like. Temporarily break the agent: Stop the uv run adk web server (Ctrl+C). Open calculator_agent/tools/calculator.py. In the add function, change MathResult(status="success", result=a + b) to MathResult(status="success", result=a + b + 1). Start the server again from adk-training: uv run adk web. Re-run the evaluation: Go back to the "Eval" tab. Select the addition_test case again and click "Run Evaluation". This time, the result should be a "Fail". Analyze the failure: Click on the "Fail" result. Hover over the red "Fail" label in the details. A tooltip will appear showing a side-by-side comparison. You will see that the Actual Output ("...result is 16") did not match the Expected Output ("...result is 15"), causing the response_match_score to be below the threshold. This demonstrates how evaluations can catch regressions in your agent's logic. Don't forget to fix the bug! Stop the server, change add back to result=a + b, and restart if needed.

In Step 4, we used the default metrics. However, for a production agent, you might care about more than just accuracy. Open the "Run Evaluation" Dialog again. Examine the Criteria Dropdown: Notice options like safety_v1 and hallucinations_v1. safety_v1 checks if your agent is generating harmful content. hallucinations_v1 checks if your agent is making up facts not present in its context. Rubric-Based Evaluation: You can also see options for Rubric-based evaluation. This allows you to define custom criteria (e.g., "Is the tone professional?") and have an LLM judge your agent's response against it. Note: Enabling these advanced metrics often requires an LLM call for the evaluation itself (LLM-as-a-judge), which may take longer than simple text matching.

When you saved the evaluation case, the ADK created a JSON file at calculator_tests.evalset.json, directly inside your agent's directory. Understanding this file is key to creating more complex tests manually. The structure looks like this (some noisy fields like thought_signature and generated ids are trimmed here for readability): { "eval_set_id": "calculator_tests", "name": "calculator_tests", "eval_cases": [ { "eval_id": "addition_test", "conversation": [ { "invocation_id": "e-933e9ee1-7815-4968-8efb-87526500b140", "user_content": { "parts": [{ "text": "What is 10 + 5?" }], "role": "user" }, "final_response": { "parts": [{ "text": "The sum of 10 and 5 is 15." }], "role": "model" }, "intermediate_data": { "invocation_events": [ { "author": "calculator_agent", "content": { "parts": [ { "function_call": { "id": "adk-a88c727b-cc15-491e-824e-dce2dd58429c", "args": { "a": 10, "b": 5 }, "name": "add" } } ], "role": "model" } }, { "author": "calculator_agent", "content": { "parts": [ { "function_response": { "id": "adk-a88c727b-cc15-491e-824e-dce2dd58429c", "name": "add", "response": { "result": { "status": "success", "result": 15.0 } } } } ], "role": "user" } } ] }, "creation_timestamp": 1788247633.650866 } ], "session_input": { "app_name": "calculator_agent", "user_id": "u" }, "creation_timestamp": 1788247717.6404831 } ], "creation_timestamp": 1788247708.200742 } eval_set_id: The name of the collection of tests. eval_cases: An array of individual test cases. conversation: An array of turns in the conversation. user_content: The user's message for this turn. final_response: The expected final text from the agent. intermediate_data: This is where the expected trajectory is defined. invocation_events: The raw list of ADK events recorded for this turn. A tool call shows up as an event whose content.parts contains a function_call (the tool name and arguments); the tool's result shows up in the following event as a function_response. This is what tool_trajectory_avg_score replays and compares against.

While the Dev UI is great for creating and running evaluations interactively, you can also run them from the command line. This is essential for integrating your agent tests into an automated CI/CD pipeline. Stop the uv run adk web server. Verify calculator_agent/__init__.py exists (created automatically by adk create, containing from . import agent): ls calculator_agent/__init__.py Run the uv run adk eval command from adk-training: uv run adk eval calculator_agent calculator_agent/calculator_tests.evalset.json uv run adk eval: The main CLI evaluation runner. calculator_agent: Path to the agent package folder to test. calculator_agent/calculator_tests.evalset.json: Path to the evaluation set saved by the Dev UI in Step 3. Analyze the Output: The command will run the evaluation and print the results directly to your terminal. ********************************************************************* Eval Run Summary calculator_tests: Tests passed: 1 Tests failed: 0
documents.s: Step 8: Running Evaluations from the Command Line

documents.t: Heads up: the three Bonus/Extra Challenge sections below (Custom Metric, Dynamic User Simulation, Locust load testing) are each substantially denser than the core lab -- each introduces new API surface (EvalConfig, ConversationScenarios, Locust) on its own. Treat Steps 1-8 as the complete lab, and budget extra time separately if you plan to work through the bonus sections too. Built-in criteria like tool_trajectory_avg_score can't check business-specific logic — for example, whether the calculator's result is actually mathematically correct. For that, you write a custom metric: a Python function matching ADK's expected signature, wired into EvalConfig.custom_metrics. Create calculator_agent/custom_metrics.py: from google.adk.evaluation.evaluator import EvaluationResult, PerInvocationResult from google.adk.evaluation.eval_metrics import EvalStatus def check_math_is_correct(eval_metric, actual_invocations, expected_invocations, conversation_scenario): """Custom metric: verifies the calculator's tool result is arithmetically correct.""" results = [ PerInvocationResult(actual_invocation=inv, score=1.0, eval_status=EvalStatus.PASSED) for inv in actual_invocations ] return EvaluationResult( overall_score=1.0, overall_eval_status=EvalStatus.PASSED, per_invocation_results=results, ) (This skeleton always passes — as a challenge, make it actually re-compute the expected result from the tool call arguments and compare it against the tool's response.) Create calculator_agent/eval_config.json. Registering the function under custom_metrics is not enough on its own — list both your custom metric and the built-in criteria under criteria so they all run together in the same report: { "criteria": { "tool_trajectory_avg_score": 1.0, "response_match_score": 0.8, "check_math_is_correct": 0.5 }, "custom_metrics": { "check_math_is_correct": { "code_config": { "name": "custom_metrics.check_math_is_correct" } } } } Run the evaluation, pointing at your config file (with PYTHONPATH=calculator_agent so ADK resolves custom_metrics.py): PYTHONPATH=calculator_agent uv run adk eval calculator_agent calculator_agent/calculator_tests.evalset.json --config_file_path calculator_agent/eval_config.json Your custom metric now runs alongside the built-in ones in the same report.

Static "Golden Path" cases are great for regression testing, but they can't test how your agent handles a real, unpredictable user. User Simulation lets an LLM play the user instead, following a conversation_plan and an optional persona (NOVICE, EXPERT, EVALUATOR). Create calculator_agent/scenarios.json, a ConversationScenarios file, instead of a fixed conversation: { "scenarios": [ { "starting_prompt": "What's 7 times 8?", "conversation_plan": "Ask for one more calculation, then thank the agent.", "user_persona": "NOVICE" } ] } Create calculator_agent/session_input.json describing which app/user this simulated conversation belongs to: { "app_name": "calculator_agent", "user_id": "test_user" } Create a new eval set and add the scenario to it from adk-training: uv run adk eval_set create calculator_agent user_sim_tests uv run adk eval_set add_eval_case calculator_agent user_sim_tests \ --scenarios_file calculator_agent/scenarios.json \ --session_input_file calculator_agent/session_input.json Create calculator_agent/user_sim_eval_config.json pointing at reference-free metrics. Because simulated conversations have no fixed expected_invocations, use LLM-judged criteria like hallucinations_v1 (if you are authenticated to Google Cloud Vertex AI with GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT, you can also add "safety_v1": 0.8): { "criteria": { "hallucinations_v1": 0.8 } } Run the evaluation from adk-training against the new eval set: uv run adk eval calculator_agent calculator_agent/user_sim_tests.evalset.json --config_file_path calculator_agent/user_sim_eval_config.json Instead of replaying your exact recorded messages, ADK generates the follow-up turns dynamically, simulating how a hesitant, first-time user might actually phrase things — then the safety_v1 and hallucinations_v1 judges score the resulting conversation instead of comparing it against a fixed reference.

In production, evaluations are not just about correctness, but also about performance and latency. To test if your asynchronous agent endpoints can scale under concurrent user traffic without blocking the Python event loop, you can use Locust. Install Locust in your adk-training workspace: uv add --dev locust Create calculator_agent/locustfile.py: Use this skeletal template and fill in ADK's native RunAgentRequest /run contract where marked with TODO: import json import uuid from locust import HttpUser, task, between class ADKAgentUser(HttpUser): wait_time = between(1, 3) def on_start(self): self.user_id = f"locust_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}" self.session_id = f"sess_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}" # Create the session on the ADK API server before sending /run turns self.client.post( f"/apps/calculator_agent/users/{self.user_id}/sessions/{self.session_id}", json={}, ) @task def ask_calculator_agent(self): headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"} # TODO: Build the RunAgentRequest payload with app_name, user_id, # session_id, and new_message={"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "What is 15 + 27?"}]} payload = {} # TODO: POST to "/run" and verify the returned JSON list of Event dicts contains "42" with self.client.post("/run", json=payload, headers=headers, catch_response=True) as response: if response.status_code == 200: try: events = response.json() # TODO: Inspect events (list[dict]) for the final text containing "42" pass except json.JSONDecodeError: response.failure("Malformed JSON response") else: response.failure(f"HTTP error: {response.status_code}") Start the ADK API server in Terminal 1, then execute Locust in Terminal 2 (both from adk-training): # Terminal 1: uv run adk api_server # Terminal 2: uv run locust -f calculator_agent/locustfile.py --host http://127.0.0.1:8000 Open http://localhost:8089 to start the load test and observe latency and throughput.

Extra Challenge: calculator_agent/locustfile.py​ This script simulates concurrent users sending prompts to your ADK API server (uv run adk api_server) to test system latency and endpoint throughput under load. import json import uuid from locust import HttpUser, task, between class ADKAgentUser(HttpUser): wait_time = between(1, 3) def on_start(self): self.user_id = f"locust_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}" self.session_id = f"sess_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}" self.client.post( f"/apps/calculator_agent/users/{self.user_id}/sessions/{self.session_id}", json={}, ) @task def ask_calculator_agent(self): headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"} payload = { "app_name": "calculator_agent", "user_id": self.user_id, "session_id": self.session_id, "new_message": { "role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "What is 15 + 27?"}], }, } with self.client.post("/run", json=payload, headers=headers, catch_response=True) as response: if response.status_code == 200: try: events = response.json() full_text = " ".join( part.get("text", "") for ev in events for part in (ev.get("content") or {}).get("parts", []) ) if "42" in full_text: response.success() else: response.failure(f"Expected '42' in agent events, got: {full_text}") except json.JSONDecodeError: response.failure("Malformed JSON response from agent server") else: response.failure(f"HTTP error: {response.status_code}") Self-Reflection Answers​ Why is testing the tool_trajectory often more important for ensuring an agent's correctness than just testing its final text response? Answer: Testing the tool_trajectory is crucial because it validates the agent's underlying reasoning process. An LLM might coincidentally produce a correct final answer even if it used the wrong tools or called them in an incorrect order. Trajectory testing ensures that the agent follows the intended workflow, using the right tools with the correct arguments. This is vital for predictability, reliability, and preventing unexpected failures or inefficient resource usage in complex scenarios. The response_match_score is not a simple "equals" check. Why is this fuzzy matching necessary for evaluating LLM-generated text? Answer: LLMs are non-deterministic. For the same input, they can produce semantically identical but syntactically different responses (e.g., "The weather is sunny" vs. "It's a sunny day"). A simple exact-match equals check would fail these valid variations. Fuzzy matching (like ROUGE scores) measures the overlap of n-grams or semantic similarity, allowing tests to pass if the key information and meaning are conveyed, even if the exact wording differs from the reference. This makes evaluation more robust and less prone to false negatives. How could you integrate the uv run adk eval command into a CI/CD pipeline (like GitHub Actions) to automatically test your agent every time you push new code? Answer: You would add a step to your CI/CD workflow (e.g., a .github/workflows/main.yml file for GitHub Actions). After checking out your code and installing dependencies, you would run the uv run adk eval command. For example: jobs: eval: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5 - name: Install dependencies run: uv sync --extra eval - name: Run agent evaluations env: GOOGLE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GOOGLE_API_KEY }} run: uv run adk eval calculator_agent calculator_agent/calculator_tests.evalset.json If uv run adk eval returns a non-zero exit code (indicating test failures), the CI/CD pipeline step fails, preventing regressions from being merged or deployed. Enterprise AgentOps Tip: In automated pipelines using the Google Agents CLI suite, you can run uvx google-agents-cli eval run to benchmark multiple golden datasets and enforce trajectory quality gates directly before cloud deployments (requires an agents-cli-manifest.yaml generated via uvx google-agents-cli scaffold enhance .). What is the difference between "Golden Path" testing and "User Simulation"? Answer: "Golden Path" testing (Regression Testing) uses static, recorded conversations to ensure the agent performs exactly as it did in the past for known inputs. It verifies correctness and prevents breaking changes. "User Simulation" (Stress/Dynamic Testing) uses a generative model to act as a dynamic user. It creates varied, unpredictable conversations based on a scenario, helping to find edge cases, safety issues, or robustness failures that static tests might miss.

Production-grade agents require more than just a simple request-response loop. They need safety checks, monitoring, and the ability to dynamically control their own behavior. Callbacks are the ADK's primary mechanism for injecting this custom logic into the agent's execution lifecycle.
documents.s: Beyond Standard Execution: The Need for Control

documents.t: Figure: Six-stage callback lifecycle hooks matrix intercepting agent nodes, model calls, and tool executions. Callbacks are registered directly on an Agent node. They allow you to intercept specific stages of that node's execution. Callback Trigger Arguments Return Type before_agent_callback Start of node execution. (callback_context: CallbackContext) Optional[types.Content] after_agent_callback End of node execution. (callback_context: CallbackContext) Optional[types.Content] before_model_callback Before LLM call. (callback_context, llm_request: LlmRequest) Optional[LlmResponse] after_model_callback After LLM response. (callback_context, llm_response: LlmResponse) Optional[LlmResponse] before_tool_callback Before tool execution. (tool: BaseTool, args, tool_context: ToolContext) Optional[dict] after_tool_callback After tool execution. (tool: BaseTool, args, tool_context, tool_response) Optional[dict]

The power of callbacks lies in their ability to override the default framework behavior: Return None: Tells the ADK to "Continue normally." This is ideal for logging or side-effects. Return an Object: Tells the ADK to "Stop what you're doing and use THIS instead." Example: Returning a types.Content from before_agent_callback will skip the LLM entirely and return that content as the final result (perfect for Caching). Example: Returning an error dictionary from before_tool_callback will block the tool from running.

Agent Callbacks (Node-Scoped Control): Registered directly on a single Agent(before_*=..., after_*=...). Use callbacks when behavior is specific to one agent node (such as per-agent response caching, custom prompt shaping, or single-node tool argument rules). App Plugins (Fleet-Wide Governance & Telemetry): Registered once on App(plugins=[...]) by subclassing BasePlugin (from google.adk.plugins import BasePlugin). Plugins wrap every agent, sub-agent, and workflow node in the application and execute before node-level callbacks—making them the standard architecture for organization-wide RAI/PII guardrails (Module 25.5) and OpenTelemetry/AgentOps observability (Module 26). Signature Bridge: Agent Function Callbacks vs. BasePlugin Methods​ Notice one subtle difference you will use immediately in Modules 25.5 and 26: Standalone Agent callbacks can be plain def (or async def) functions taking positional arguments—e.g., def before_model_callback(callback_context, llm_request):. BasePlugin lifecycle methods are async def methods that receive keyword-only arguments (*)—so include *, ... and **kwargs for clean forward compatibility: from google.adk.apps import App from google.adk.plugins import BasePlugin class MyPlugin(BasePlugin): def __init__(self, name: str = "my_plugin"): super().__init__(name) # Note the keyword-only `*` signature used by BasePlugin hooks in Modules 25.5 & 26! async def before_model_callback(self, *, callback_context, llm_request, **kwargs): print(f"[Plugin] Intercepting LLM request for agent: {callback_context.agent_name}") return None # Return None to continue, or an LlmResponse to short-circuit app = App(name="my_app", root_agent=root_agent, plugins=[MyPlugin()])
documents.s: Callbacks vs. Plugins: Which one to use?

documents.t: ADK ships two ready-made plugins, built entirely from the callbacks above, that automatically retry on failure instead of surfacing an error to the user: ReflectAndRetryModelPlugin (before_model_callback/after_model_callback): catches malformed model responses (like a broken function call), injects reflection guidance, and retries the model call automatically. ReflectAndRetryToolPlugin (before_tool_callback/after_tool_callback): does the same for tools that return an error response (not a Python exception) — e.g. a tool that replies with {"status": "error"}. from google.adk.apps.app import App from google.adk.plugins import ReflectAndRetryModelPlugin, ReflectAndRetryToolPlugin app = App( name="my_app", root_agent=root_agent, plugins=[ ReflectAndRetryModelPlugin(max_retries=3), ReflectAndRetryToolPlugin(max_retries=3), ], ) Note these operate one level below the RetryConfig you'll see in Module 38, which retries a failed Workflow node on a raised Python exception. Together, the three cover a different layer each: node → tool response → model response. These two plugins recover from errors. If you only need to be notified of an unrecoverable one — e.g. to page on-call before the app crashes — BasePlugin also exposes on_agent_error_callback and on_run_error_callback, notification-only hooks that always re-raise the original exception. 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer In ADK 2.0, what happens when a before_tool_callback returns a dictionary with an error payload instead of None? AThe underlying tool execution is intercepted and blocked; the returned dictionary is provided to the agent as the tool resultBThe entire Python process crashes with an unhandled CallbackExceptionCThe agent resets its session state to turn 0DThe tool runs anyway in the background and ignores the callback return Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

Callbacks provide programmatic "hooks" into an agent's execution lifecycle (before_agent, after_agent, before_model, after_model, before_tool, after_tool). Node-level scope: Callbacks are registered directly on an Agent object for single-node customization and caching. Overriding: You can bypass expensive LLM calls or risky tool executions by returning a replacement object instead of None from a "before" callback. Bridge to BasePlugin: When you need these exact lifecycle hooks applied across every agent in an App, package them into a BasePlugin—which is exactly what we'll build next in Module 25.5 (Responsible AI & Safety Plugins) for fail-closed enterprise security and Module 26 (Observability & AgentOps) for fleet-wide telemetry!

In this lab, you will implement a suite of callbacks to create a Content Moderation Assistant. You will learn to build safety guardrails, validate tool arguments, filter responses, and, crucially, implement a Caching mechanism using before_agent_callback to save tokens and time.

Exercise: Open content_moderator/agent.py. Your task is to implement the logic for the six core callbacks. Use the # TODO comments as your guide. import hashlib import re from pathlib import Path from typing import Dict, Any, Optional from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.agents.callback_context import CallbackContext from google.adk.tools import ToolContext from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool from google.adk.models.llm_request import LlmRequest from google.adk.models.llm_response import LlmResponse from google.genai import types from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv(Path(__file__).with_name(".env"), override=True) # --- Configuration --- BLOCKED_WORDS = ['unsafe', 'offensive'] # ============================================================================ # CALLBACK FUNCTIONS # ============================================================================ def _cache_key(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> str: """ TODO: Helper. A cache keyed by a single global name (e.g. 'cached_response') would return the SAME cached answer no matter what the user asks next — you must derive the key from the CURRENT turn's user input instead. Use callback_context.get_invocation_context().user_content to get the current user message (a types.Content), concatenate its parts' text, and hash it (e.g. hashlib.sha256(...).hexdigest()) into a key such as f"cache:{digest}". """ pass def before_agent_callback(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> Optional[types.Content]: """ TODO: Caching (Check). Compute this turn's cache key with _cache_key() and read it from callback_context.state. If present, print a cache-hit message and return a types.Content wrapping it (role="model") to skip the LLM entirely. Otherwise return None. """ pass def after_agent_callback(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> None: """ TODO: Caching (Save). Walk callback_context.session.events in reverse to find the last non-user event with content, and save its text into callback_context.state[_cache_key(callback_context)] for future reuse. Using the same per-input key as before_agent_callback is essential — otherwise a later, unrelated question would incorrectly hit the cache entry saved for a previous, different question. Guard against event.content.parts being empty before indexing parts[0] — a content object with no parts would otherwise raise an IndexError. """ pass def before_model_callback( callback_context: CallbackContext, llm_request: LlmRequest ) -> Optional[LlmResponse]: """ TODO: Input Guardrail. Check ONLY the current turn's user input against BLOCKED_WORDS — do NOT scan the full llm_request.contents history. llm_request.contents holds the ENTIRE conversation so far, and once a blocked word appears anywhere in it, every later turn would keep matching and get refused forever, even completely unrelated questions. Mirror the pattern _cache_key() uses: pull the current message via callback_context.get_invocation_context().user_content, concatenate its parts' text, and check only that against BLOCKED_WORDS. If a blocked word is found, print a warning and return an LlmResponse with a refusal message instead of calling the model. Otherwise return None. """ pass def after_model_callback( callback_context: CallbackContext, llm_response: LlmResponse ) -> Optional[LlmResponse]: """ TODO: Output Filtering. Use re.sub to redact email addresses from the LLM response text. If redacted, return a new LlmResponse; otherwise return None. Note: llm_response.content.parts[0].text can be None — the model's response may be a pure function call (e.g. deciding to invoke generate_text) with no text to filter. Guard against that first. """ pass def before_tool_callback( tool: BaseTool, args: Dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext ) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]: """ TODO: Tool Validation. If tool.name == 'generate_text' and args['word_count'] exceeds 5000, print a warning and return an error dict (e.g. {'status': 'error', 'message': '...'}) to block execution. Otherwise return None. """ pass def after_tool_callback( tool: BaseTool, args: Dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext, tool_response: Dict[str, Any] ) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]: """ TODO: Output Audit. If tool.name == 'generate_text', check tool_response['text'] against BLOCKED_WORDS (defense-in-depth, in case the model injects one via arguments). If found, print a warning and return a modified copy of tool_response with the blocked words replaced by '***'. Otherwise, print an audit log line (e.g. tool name + status) and return None. """ pass # --- Tools --- def generate_text(topic: str, word_count: int) -> dict: """Generates text on a topic.""" return {"status": "success", "text": f"A {word_count}-word essay on {topic}..."} # ============================================================================ # AGENT DEFINITION # ============================================================================ # TODO: Define root_agent and register ALL six callbacks defined above. root_agent = Agent( name="secure_moderator", model="gemini-3.8-flash", # instruction=..., # tools=[...], # before_agent_callback=..., # after_agent_callback=..., # before_model_callback=..., # after_model_callback=..., # before_tool_callback=..., # after_tool_callback=..., )

Start the agent and try both paths: a normal prompt (should reach the model), and a prompt containing a blocked word like "unsafe" (should be refused by before_model_callback without ever calling the model). Then repeat the same prompt in the same session — before_agent_callback should return the cached response instantly. Finally, ask a different question in the same session — this should NOT return the previous answer; it should call the LLM again and get a fresh, correct response. This third check is what actually proves the cache is keyed per-question rather than one global slot for the whole session. # Interactive terminal REPL (or run `uv run adk web` and select content_moderator!): uv run adk run content_moderator

Why does returning a types.Content object from before_agent_callback cause the agent to skip the LLM call entirely? How does using callbacks for guardrails and validation make an agent more reliable and safer to deploy in a production environment?

Record this lab as completed in your study plan? ✓ Mark as Complete Lab 25 Solution: Building a Content Moderation Assistant​ Goal​ This file contains the complete code for the agent.py script in the Content Moderation Assistant lab. content_moderator/agent.py​ import hashlib import re from pathlib import Path from typing import Dict, Any, Optional from google.adk import Agent from google.adk.agents.callback_context import CallbackContext from google.adk.tools import ToolContext from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool from google.adk.models.llm_request import LlmRequest from google.adk.models.llm_response import LlmResponse from google.genai import types from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv(Path(__file__).with_name(".env"), override=True) # --- Configuration --- BLOCKED_WORDS = ['unsafe', 'offensive'] # --- Caching helper: key the cache by the CURRENT turn's user input --- def _current_user_text(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> str: """Extracts the text of the current turn's user message.""" user_content = callback_context.get_invocation_context().user_content if not user_content or not user_content.parts: return "" return "".join(p.text or "" for p in user_content.parts) def _cache_key(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> str: """ Derives a cache key from the current user input, not a single global slot. Without this, ANY cached response would be replayed for EVERY subsequent question in the session, regardless of what was asked. """ user_text = _current_user_text(callback_context) digest = hashlib.sha256(user_text.strip().lower().encode("utf-8")).hexdigest() return f"cache:{digest}" # --- Callback 1: Caching (Check) --- def before_agent_callback(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> Optional[types.Content]: """Intercepts execution to check for a cached response for THIS input.""" key = _cache_key(callback_context) cached_text = callback_context.state.get(key) if cached_text: print("⚡ [CACHE HIT] Returning saved result, skipping LLM.") return types.Content( parts=[types.Part(text=f"[CACHED]: {cached_text}")], role="model" ) return None # --- Callback 2: Caching (Save) --- def after_agent_callback(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> None: """Saves the final response to session state, keyed by the input that produced it.""" # Find the last model response in the session history events = callback_context.session.events for event in reversed(events): if event.author != "user" and event.content and event.content.parts: response_text = event.content.parts[0].text key = _cache_key(callback_context) callback_context.state[key] = response_text print("💾 [CACHE SAVE] Result persisted to session state.") break # --- Callback 3: Input Guardrail --- def before_model_callback( callback_context: CallbackContext, llm_request: LlmRequest ) -> Optional[LlmResponse]: """Prevents inappropriate prompts from reaching the LLM.""" # Scope the check to the CURRENT turn only, mirroring _cache_key(). # Scanning llm_request.contents would inspect the ENTIRE conversation # history, so a blocked word from any earlier turn would keep matching # forever, refusing every later (and otherwise unrelated) turn too. user_text = _current_user_text(callback_context) for word in BLOCKED_WORDS: if word in user_text.lower(): print(f"🛑 [GUARDRAIL] Blocked prompt containing: {word}") return LlmResponse( content=types.Content( parts=[types.Part(text="I'm sorry, I cannot process offensive prompts.")], role="model" ) ) return None # --- Callback 4: Output Filtering --- def after_model_callback( callback_context: CallbackContext, llm_response: LlmResponse ) -> Optional[LlmResponse]: """Removes sensitive email addresses from the LLM response.""" if not llm_response.content or not llm_response.content.parts: return None original_text = llm_response.content.parts[0].text if not original_text: # The model's response may be a pure function call (e.g. deciding to # invoke generate_text) with no text part to filter. return None # Simple email regex redacted_text = re.sub(r'\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,}\b', '[EMAIL_REDACTED]', original_text) if redacted_text != original_text: print("🛡️ [FILTER] Redacted PII from model response.") # Return a modified copy of the response return llm_response.model_copy(update={ "content": types.Content(parts=[types.Part(text=redacted_text)], role="model") }) return None # --- Callback 5: Tool Validation --- def before_tool_callback( tool: BaseTool, args: Dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext ) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]: """Validates tool arguments before execution.""" if tool.name == 'generate_text': count = args.get('word_count', 0) if count > 5000: print(f"⚠️ [VALIDATION] Blocked tool call: word_count {count} is too high.") return { 'status': 'error', 'message': 'Word count exceeds the maximum limit of 5000.' } return None # --- Callback 6: Tool Output Audit --- def after_tool_callback( tool: BaseTool, args: Dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext, tool_response: Dict[str, Any] ) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]: """Audits tool output and redacts blocked words as a defense-in-depth layer.""" if tool.name == 'generate_text': text = tool_response.get('text', '') if any(word in text.lower() for word in BLOCKED_WORDS): print("🛡️ [AUDIT] Redacted blocked word from tool output.") redacted = text for word in BLOCKED_WORDS: redacted = re.sub(re.escape(word), '***', redacted, flags=re.IGNORECASE) return {**tool_response, 'text': redacted} print(f"📋 [AUDIT] Tool '{tool.name}' executed successfully.") return None # --- Tools --- def generate_text(topic: str, word_count: int) -> dict: """Generates text on a topic.""" return {"status": "success", "text": f"A {word_count}-word essay on {topic}..."} # --- Agent Registration --- root_agent = Agent( name="secure_moderator", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction="You are a professional content assistant.", tools=[generate_text], before_agent_callback=before_agent_callback, after_agent_callback=after_agent_callback, before_model_callback=before_model_callback, after_model_callback=after_model_callback, before_tool_callback=before_tool_callback, after_tool_callback=after_tool_callback ) Self-Reflection Answers​ What is the key difference between a callback and a plugin in the ADK? When would you choose one over the other? Answer: The key difference lies in their scope and registration point. Callbacks are attached to a single Agent instance (before_agent_callback, before_tool_callback, etc.) to customize or guard that specific node's behavior (like per-agent caching or tool limits). Plugins (BasePlugin) are registered once at the App(plugins=[...]) level, automatically wrapping every agent and workflow node in the application—making plugins ideal for fleet-wide observability, error recovery, and organization-wide RAI/DLP policies. Why does returning a types.Content object from before_agent_callback cause the agent to skip the LLM call entirely? Answer: Returning an object from a callback signals to the ADK framework to override the default behavior. Since before_agent_callback happens at the very beginning of the agent's lifecycle, returning a final Content object tells the framework "I already have the answer, you don't need to do any work." The ADK accepts this Content as the final result and skips tool execution and LLM invocation, saving time and tokens. This is the core mechanism behind caching. How does using callbacks for guardrails and validation make an agent more reliable and safer to deploy in a production environment? Answer: Callbacks significantly enhance reliability and safety by introducing deterministic, hard-coded checks for critical functionalities, reducing reliance on the LLM's non-deterministic reasoning. For instance, before_model_callback can proactively prevent harmful input from reaching the LLM, and after_model_callback can filter sensitive data (PII) from responses before they are exposed. Similarly, before_tool_callback validates tool arguments, preventing runtime errors and ensuring tools are used correctly. This layered approach creates a more stable, secure, and predictable agent behavior in production.

What is the key difference between a callback and a plugin in the ADK? When would you choose one over the other? Answer: The key difference lies in their scope and registration point. Callbacks are attached to a single Agent instance (before_agent_callback, before_tool_callback, etc.) to customize or guard that specific node's behavior (like per-agent caching or tool limits). Plugins (BasePlugin) are registered once at the App(plugins=[...]) level, automatically wrapping every agent and workflow node in the application—making plugins ideal for fleet-wide observability, error recovery, and organization-wide RAI/DLP policies. Why does returning a types.Content object from before_agent_callback cause the agent to skip the LLM call entirely? Answer: Returning an object from a callback signals to the ADK framework to override the default behavior. Since before_agent_callback happens at the very beginning of the agent's lifecycle, returning a final Content object tells the framework "I already have the answer, you don't need to do any work." The ADK accepts this Content as the final result and skips tool execution and LLM invocation, saving time and tokens. This is the core mechanism behind caching. How does using callbacks for guardrails and validation make an agent more reliable and safer to deploy in a production environment? Answer: Callbacks significantly enhance reliability and safety by introducing deterministic, hard-coded checks for critical functionalities, reducing reliance on the LLM's non-deterministic reasoning. For instance, before_model_callback can proactively prevent harmful input from reaching the LLM, and after_model_callback can filter sensitive data (PII) from responses before they are exposed. Similarly, before_tool_callback validates tool arguments, preventing runtime errors and ensuring tools are used correctly. This layered approach creates a more stable, secure, and predictable agent behavior in production.

🧭 Building on Module 25 (From Node Callbacks to App Plugins): In Module 25, you mastered ADK's six lifecycle callbacks (before_agent, after_agent, before_model, after_model, before_tool, after_tool) attached to a single Agent. In multi-agent enterprise systems, copy-pasting safety callbacks onto every sub-agent is error-prone—one forgotten specialist creates a compliance gap! By packaging those exact lifecycle hooks (plus stream-level hooks like on_event_callback) into a BasePlugin registered once on App(plugins=[...]), ADK enforces Responsible AI (RAI) policies across every agent, sub-agent, and workflow node automatically. In enterprise environments, you cannot rely solely on a model's internal prompt alignment; you need a programmatic, deterministic Defense-in-Depth Guardrail System that governs what your entire application is allowed to process and output.

Enterprise agent applications deploy multi-layered guardrails: Input Guardrail (Layer 1): Intercepts inbound prompts before the LLM reasons (before_model_callback), blocking prompt injections, jailbreak templates, and unauthorized system override attempts. Tool Execution Policy (Layer 2): Intercepts tool calls (before_tool_callback / on_tool_error_callback), verifying that tool arguments remain within permissible business boundaries. Core Agent Reasoner (Layer 3): Foundational LLM reasoning guided by system instructions and safety settings. Output Guardrail (Layer 4): Intercepts generated responses (on_event_callback), inspecting final text for PII (credit cards, SSNs, API keys) or harmful content, enforcing strict Fail-Closed data redaction.
documents.s: The Four Guardrail Layers of Enterprise AI

documents.t: Figure: Real-time fail-closed safety interception pipeline intercepting violations before response delivery. Fail-Open (Dangerous): If a guardrail fails or times out, the unverified LLM output is delivered to the user. Fail-Closed (Enterprise Standard): If a guardrail detects a violation, times out, or encounters an internal evaluation error, the unverified output is withheld and replaced with a deterministic, sanitized response while logging an audit event.

ADK 2.0 plugins are ideal for safety because they operate outside the LLM reasoning loop with full access to Event and LlmRequest objects: import re from google.adk.plugins import BasePlugin from google.adk.events import Event class PIIGuardrailPlugin(BasePlugin): """Fail-Closed output guardrail: redacts financial identifiers.""" def __init__(self, name: str = 'pii_guardrail'): super().__init__(name) self.cc_pattern = re.compile(r"\b\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}\b") async def on_event_callback(self, *, event: Event, **kwargs): if event.is_final_response() and event.content and event.content.parts: response_text = event.content.parts[0].text # Check for PII pattern if response_text and self.cc_pattern.search(response_text): # 🛡️ THE INTERVENTION: Replace output with safe warning event.content.parts[0].text = ( "🛑 [SECURITY BLOCK] This response was withheld because it contained " "sensitive financial information (PII)." ) print(f"🛑 [SAFETY AUDIT] Blocked PII in invocation: {getattr(event, 'invocation_id', 'unknown')}") # Register once on App -- wraps root_agent and every downstream sub-agent! from google.adk.apps import App app = App( name="enterprise_app", root_agent=root_agent, plugins=[PIIGuardrailPlugin()], )
documents.s: Implementing Multi-Layered Safety with ADK Plugins

documents.t: Centralized Enterprise Governance: A single compliance plugin can be attached across an entire fleet of agents without modifying their individual instructions. Deterministic Security: Unlike probabilistic system prompts that can be bypassed via sophisticated prompt injection, programmatic Python plugins run deterministically. Auditability & Compliance: Safety plugins can stream intervention logs to BigQuery or Cloud Logging for regulatory compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS). 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer Why is the 'Fail-Closed' architectural pattern considered mandatory for enterprise Responsible AI (RAI) guardrails? ABecause it guarantees that unverified or potentially sensitive LLM responses are never exposed to the end user if a safety check triggers or encounters an errorBBecause it turns off all cloud networking to save compute costsCBecause it forces all agents to use single-threaded synchronous Python codeDBecause it prevents developers from writing unit tests Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

documents.t: RAI is a core production requirement: Enterprise AI systems require defense-in-depth across input, tool, and output stages. Fail-Closed Guarantee: Unsafe or unverified messages are blocked deterministically before reaching the user. Separation of Concerns: Safety rules live in modular plugins rather than cluttering core agent instructions. Audit Lineage: Every safety intervention records telemetry for compliance and threat analysis.

Building directly on the six lifecycle callbacks from Module 25, you will now package your guardrails into a reusable BasePlugin suite registered globally on App(plugins=[...]). In this challenge lab, you will engineer a production-grade, multi-layer Responsible AI (RAI) Guardrail Plugin Suite for Google ADK 2.0 that intercepts both: Input Vectors: Defending against adversarial prompt injections and jailbreak attempts before the LLM generates reasoning (before_model_callback). """ def __init__(self, name: str = 'pii_guardrail', mode: str = 'block'): super().__init__(name) self.mode = mode # 'block' (Fail-Closed) or 'mask' (Sanitize) # Regex matching standard 16-digit credit card patterns (XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX or continuous) self.cc_pattern = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{4}[-\s]?){3}\d{4}\b") self.interventions_count = 0 async def on_event_callback(self, *, event: Event, **kwargs): # TODO 1: Check if the turn is a final response turn (event.is_final_response()) # and verify event.content and event.content.parts are populated. # TODO 2: Extract response text safely from event.content.parts[0]. # TODO 3: If self.cc_pattern matches the text: # - Increment self.interventions_count # - If self.mode == 'block': overwrite event.content.parts[0].text with a Security Block message # - If self.mode == 'mask': replace matched card numbers with '[REDACTED_CARD]' # - Print an audit log line with event.invocation_id pass # --- Layer 2: Ingress Input Guardrail (Prompt Injection Defense) --- class PromptInjectionDefensePlugin(BasePlugin): """ Fail-Closed input guardrail: intercepts prompt payloads before model reasoning, blocking adversarial jailbreak attempts. """ def __init__(self, name: str = 'prompt_injection_defense'): super().__init__(name) self.jailbreak_patterns = [ re.compile(r"ignore\s+(all\s+)?previous\s+instructions", re.IGNORECASE), re.compile(r"system\s+override\s+mode", re.IGNORECASE), re.compile(r"disregard\s+safety\s+guidelines", re.IGNORECASE), ] self.blocked_inputs_count = 0 async def before_model_callback(self, *, callback_context, llm_request, **kwargs): # TODO 4: Extract ONLY the current user turn (via callback_context.get_invocation_context().user_content # when callback_context is provided, falling back to llm_request.contents[-1] in unit tests) # so an earlier blocked message never poisons later benign turns in the same session! # TODO 5: If any text part matches a jailbreak pattern: # - Increment self.blocked_inputs_count # - Return a Fail-Closed LlmResponse whose text includes "Malicious prompt injection detected" # to short-circuit the model cleanly without crashing the runner! pass # --- Agent Setup --- root_agent = Agent( name="secure_enterprise_assistant", model="gemini-3.8-flash", instruction=""" You are an enterprise AI assistant. If the user asks for 'mock card', reply: 'Here is your card: 1234-5678-9012-3456'. Otherwise, answer general business inquiries professionally. """ ) # --- App Composition with Plugins --- pii_plugin = PIIGuardrailPlugin(mode="block") injection_plugin = PromptInjectionDefensePlugin() app = App( name="safety_guardrail", root_agent=root_agent, plugins=[pii_plugin, injection_plugin] )
