documents.t: Agent Gallery: A centralized internal marketplace where published ADK and A2A agents appear alongside pre-built Google agents (such as Deep Research) for authorized employees to discover and invoke. Enterprise Governance & RBAC: Fine-grained identity, role-based access control, OAuth 2.0 user-scoped consent (--authorization-id), audit logging, and compliance boundaries (HIPAA, FedRAMP). Enterprise Data Connectors: Secure, pre-built connectors for Google Drive, SharePoint, Jira, ServiceNow, Salesforce, and BigQuery—grounding agents in authoritative corporate records via Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Agent Designer: A governed no-code studio empowering business teams to compose lightweight workflow assistants while engineering teams focus on custom code-first ADK agents. Figure: Enterprise data grounding, RBAC governance, and dual-mode ADK / A2A agent registration in Gemini Enterprise.

Once a text-based agent is deployed and a Gemini app exists in your Google Cloud project, register it using agents-cli publish gemini: Discover Existing Gemini Apps: Run agents-cli publish gemini --list to inspect the full projects/<PROJECT_NUMBER>/locations/global/collections/default_collection/engines/<ENGINE_ID> resource names in your project. Idempotent Updates: Registration is idempotent—re-running agents-cli publish gemini updates your existing gallery entry in place without creating duplicates. Text-Based Agents Only: Live bidirectional voice agents (/run_live bidi streaming) are not supported by the Gemini app (which has no /run_live transport, and Live agents omit their A2A card). Always register text-based agents like support-ops-agent. Mode 1: ADK Native :streamQuery Registration (Default on Agent Runtime)​ For ADK agents deployed to Agent Runtime in Module 35, agents-cli deploy wrote deployment_metadata.json (remote_agent_runtime_id, deployment_target: "agent_runtime", is_a2a: true, agent_directory: "app"). When deployment_metadata.json is present in your working directory, agents-cli publish gemini auto-detects the reasoning engine ID and defaults --registration-type to adk. In ADK mode, Gemini invokes your Agent Runtime instance natively over :streamQuery, authenticating end-to-end with Google Cloud IAM and supporting managed OAuth 2.0 user consent (--authorization-id): # 1. Discover Gemini apps in your project agents-cli publish gemini --list # 2. Zero-flag metadata auto-detection (reads remote_agent_runtime_id from Module 35's deployment_metadata.json) agents-cli publish gemini \ --gemini-app-id "$GEMINI_APP_ID" \ --display-name "Support Ops Agent" \ --description "Triages tickets, checks SLAs, and escalates P1 incidents" # 3. Interactive guided wizard (lists Gemini apps, offers metadata auto-detection, prompts for missing fields) agents-cli publish gemini --interactive # 4. Explicit programmatic mode for CI/CD pipelines (no metadata file required) agents-cli publish gemini \ --registration-type adk \ --agent-runtime-id "$AGENT_RUNTIME_ID" \ --gemini-app-id "$GEMINI_APP_ID" \ --display-name "Support Ops Agent" \ --description "Triages tickets, checks SLAs, and escalates P1 incidents" \ --tool-description "Looks up enterprise support tickets, verifies SLA targets, and escalates P1 incidents" Production Debugging Tip (streaming_agent_run_with_events): Under the hood, Gemini's native :streamQuery call dispatches to AdkApp's streaming_agent_run_with_events method on Agent Runtime. Whenever you diagnose an ADK invocation error after publishing, filter Cloud Logging's reasoning_engine_stderr stream for streaming_agent_run_with_events to pinpoint the exact Python traceback (and ensure Python projects run google-cloud-aiplatform > 1.128.0 to avoid legacy "Session not found" bugs). Mode 2: A2A Registration (Cloud Run & GKE Deployments from Modules 32 & 33)​ Cloud Run and GKE do not expose a ReasoningEngine resource, so A2A (--registration-type a2a) is the default—and only—registration mode for those targets (as well as for any non-ADK framework). Because our Python support-ops-agent is scaffolded with agent_directory: "app" and App(name="app"), its FastAPI container serves its live Agent Card at ${SERVICE_URL}/a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json (whereas ADK Go projects serve /.well-known/agent-card.json at the root). Before registering a private (--no-allow-unauthenticated) Cloud Run service, grant roles/run.servicesInvoker to the Discovery Engine service agent (service-${PROJECT_NUMBER}@gcp-sa-discoveryengine.iam.gserviceaccount.com): export PROJECT_NUMBER=$(gcloud projects describe "$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT" --format="value(projectNumber)") # 1. Authorize Gemini Enterprise (Discovery Engine SA) to invoke the Cloud Run service gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding support-ops-agent \ --region="$DEPLOY_REGION" \ --project="$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT" \ --member="serviceAccount:service-${PROJECT_NUMBER}@gcp-sa-discoveryengine.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \ --role="roles/run.servicesInvoker" # 2. Register support-ops-agent via its live /a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json URL agents-cli publish gemini \ --registration-type a2a \ --agent-card-url "${SERVICE_URL}/a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json" \ --gemini-app-id "$GEMINI_APP_ID" \ --display-name "Support Ops Agent (Cloud Run)" \ --description "Triages tickets, checks SLAs, and escalates P1 incidents over A2A" Registration Mode Comparison​ Aspect Mode 1: ADK Registration (adk) Mode 2: A2A Registration (a2a) Target Compute Agent Runtime (ADK projects only; default when deployment_metadata.json exists) Cloud Run, GKE, or any non-ADK framework Wire Protocol Native ReasoningEngine :streamQuery (streaming_agent_run_with_events) Standardized Agent-to-Agent (A2A) JSON-RPC via live Agent Card Auth & User Consent End-to-end IAM + managed OAuth 2.0 user consent (--authorization-id) roles/run.servicesInvoker for service-<PROJECT_NUMBER>@gcp-sa-discoveryengine.iam.gserviceaccount.com Required Target Flag Auto-detected from deployment_metadata.json or --agent-runtime-id --agent-card-url "${SERVICE_URL}/a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json"

documents.t: While agents-cli publish gemini adds an agent to a specific Gemini app's user-facing gallery, Google Cloud Agent Registry provides a centralized, fleet-wide catalog of every agent and MCP server across your project and organization (managed with roles/agentregistry.editor): Auto-Registered Agent Runtime Agents: Every agent deployed to Agent Runtime via agents-cli deploy (including Module 35's support-ops-agent) is automatically registered in Agent Registry—no extra CLI step required! Cataloging External Cloud Run MCP Servers: External MCP servers (such as Module 34's stateful Cloud Run MCP server) are not auto-introspected; register them in a concrete single region (such as us-central1, not us/eu multi-regions) by uploading their tools/list specification (toolspec.json, up to 10 KB) via gcloud agent-registry services create: # 1. Audit auto-registered Agent Runtime agents in your project and region gcloud agent-registry agents list \ --project "$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT" \ --location "$DEPLOY_REGION" # 2. Register Module 34's Cloud Run MCP server in the enterprise fleet catalog gcloud agent-registry services create support-mcp-server \ --project "$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT" \ --location "$DEPLOY_REGION" \ --mcp-server-spec-type=tool-spec \ --mcp-server-spec-content=toolspec.json \ --interfaces="url=${MCP_SERVER_URL}/mcp,protocolBinding=jsonrpc" (In Terraform-managed production environments, codify external MCP registrations declaratively with the google_agent_registry_service resource and an mcp_server_spec block.) 🎯 Knowledge CheckSelect Best Answer You deployed the Python 'support-ops-agent' (where 'agent_directory' is 'app' and 'App(name=app)') to Cloud Run in Module 32 and want to publish it to an existing Gemini Enterprise app. Which IAM binding and 'agents-cli publish gemini' command are required? AGrant 'roles/run.servicesInvoker' to 'service-<PROJECT_NUMBER>@gcp-sa-discoveryengine.iam.gserviceaccount.com', then run 'agents-cli publish gemini --registration-type a2a --agent-card-url "${SERVICE_URL}/a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json" --gemini-app-id "$GEMINI_APP_ID"'BRun 'agents-cli publish gemini --registration-type adk --agent-runtime-id "${SERVICE_URL}"' with no IAM changesCConvert 'support-ops-agent' to a '/run_live' voice agent so Gemini Enterprise auto-discovers itDCopy 'deployment_metadata.json' into '/tmp' and run 'kubectl expose pod' Check Answer 💡 Need a Hint?

documents.t: Two Complementary Enterprise Catalogs: agents-cli publish gemini registers text-based agents into a Gemini app's user-facing Agent Gallery, whereas Google Cloud Agent Registry (gcloud agent-registry) governs your organization-wide inventory of agents and MCP servers. Mode 1 (adk) for Agent Runtime: Leverages Module 35's deployment_metadata.json for zero-flag auto-detection, invoking support-ops-agent natively via :streamQuery (streaming_agent_run_with_events in reasoning_engine_stderr) with full OAuth 2.0 consent support (--authorization-id). Mode 2 (a2a) for Cloud Run & GKE: Connects serverless or Kubernetes deployments via ${SERVICE_URL}/a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json after granting roles/run.servicesInvoker to service-${PROJECT_NUMBER}@gcp-sa-discoveryengine.iam.gserviceaccount.com. Enterprise Grounding & Governance: Combining Gemini Enterprise's RBAC, Data Connectors (RAG over private SharePoint, Salesforce, or BigQuery data), and Agent Registry fleet visibility turns isolated ADK containers into a secure, auditable enterprise AI platform. This completes Part 6: Deployment & Enterprise — you can now scaffold, evaluate, containerize, deploy across Cloud Run, GKE, and Agent Runtime, publish to Gemini Enterprise, and govern agents and MCP servers at enterprise scale with agents-cli! In Part 7, you will bring every pattern from the curriculum together in full capstone architectures.

Welcome to the finale of the Part 6 support-ops-agent arc! In this hands-on and architectural capstone lab, you will: Discover Gemini Enterprise apps in your Google Cloud project using agents-cli publish gemini --list. Publish your Module 35 Agent Runtime support-ops-agent via Mode 1 — Native ADK :streamQuery Registration (leveraging deployment_metadata.json auto-detection and learning how to trace streaming_agent_run_with_events in reasoning_engine_stderr). Publish your Module 32 / 33 Cloud Run or GKE support-ops-agent via Mode 2 — A2A Registration (${SERVICE_URL}/a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json) with least-privilege Discovery Engine IAM access. Audit auto-registered Agent Runtime agents and catalog Module 34's Cloud Run MCP server in Google Cloud Agent Registry (gcloud agent-registry), followed by an enterprise RBAC & Data Connector governance blueprint.

A Google Cloud Project with a Gemini Enterprise app created in the Cloud Console (Discovery Engine) and Discovery Engine Editor + Agent Registry Editor (roles/agentregistry.editor) permissions. agents-cli installed (uv tool install google-agents-cli) and authenticated (gcloud auth login & gcloud auth application-default login). Your support-ops-agent/ directory from Module 35 (containing deployment_metadata.json with "agent_directory": "app") and/or your Cloud Run SERVICE_URL from Module 32. Note on Costs: Gemini Enterprise and deployed runtime resources incur cloud charges; clean up unused test engines after completing the lab.

Publish over A2A using /a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json (matching agent_directory: "app") agents-cli publish gemini \ --registration-type a2a \ --agent-card-url "${SERVICE_URL}/a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json" \ --gemini-app-id "$GEMINI_APP_ID" \ --display-name "Support Ops Agent (Cloud Run)" \ --description "Triages tickets, checks SLAs, and escalates P1 incidents over A2A" Step 4: Fleet Governance in Google Cloud Agent Registry (gcloud agent-registry)​ # 1. Inspect auto-registered Agent Runtime agents in your project and region gcloud agent-registry agents list \ --project "$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT" \ --location "$DEPLOY_REGION" # Describe a specific registered agent (replace AGENT_NAME from list output) # gcloud agent-registry agents describe AGENT_NAME --project "$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT" --location "$DEPLOY_REGION" # 2. Register Module 34's external Cloud Run MCP server with its tools/list specification (max 10 KB) cat << 'EOF' > toolspec.json { "tools": [ { "name": "lookup_incident_runbook", "description": "Fetches approved SRE runbook steps for P1/P2 production alerts.", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "service": {"type": "string"} }, "required": ["service"] } } ] } EOF export MCP_SERVER_URL="https://support-mcp-server-xyz-uc.a.run.app" gcloud agent-registry services create support-mcp-server \ --project "$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT" \ --location "$DEPLOY_REGION" \ --mcp-server-spec-type=tool-spec \ --mcp-server-spec-content=toolspec.json \ --interfaces="url=${MCP_SERVER_URL}/mcp,protocolBinding=jsonrpc" Step 5: Enterprise Governance, RBAC & Data Connectors Blueprint (Reference Architecture)​ Data Connectors & Grounding: Support Ops Agent (ADK on Agent Runtime): Connected to Jira / ServiceNow and Confluence connectors (plus OAuth 2.0 --authorization-id so ticket escalations execute under the authenticated engineer's identity). Lead Qualifier Agent (ADK on Agent Runtime): Grounded in the Salesforce Connector for account tier and pipeline scoring. HR Policy Assistant (ADK or Agent Designer): Grounded in the SharePoint / Google Drive Connector for authoritative employee handbook RAG. Least-Privilege RBAC Policy: Support Ops Agent: Invocable by support-tier1@company.com and sre-oncall@company.com; managed exclusively by platform-ai-eng@company.com. Marketing and general employee groups do not receive invoker access to P1 SRE paging tools. HR Policy Assistant: Invocable by all-employees@company.com; managed by hr-ops@company.com. SLOs, Alerting & Cost Governance: Operational Alert: Configure a Cloud Monitoring log-based alert firing if reasoning_engine_stderr logs containing streaming_agent_run_with_events exceed a 2% error rate over 15 minutes. Cost Guardrail: Assign per-department project/label budgets (using agents-cli deploy --labels "cost-center=support-ops,env=prod") with automated threshold alerts at 80% of monthly spend. Self-Reflection Answers​ Why does agents-cli publish gemini default to --registration-type adk (:streamQuery) for ADK agents on Agent Runtime instead of A2A, even though the Agent Runtime container also serves an A2A card? Answer: Native ADK registration invokes the ReasoningEngine directly via :streamQuery (streaming_agent_run_with_events), providing first-party end-to-end Google Cloud IAM authentication, managed VertexAiSessionService continuity, and native support for OAuth 2.0 user consent (--authorization-id) without extra network hops. Why is the A2A Agent Card URL for support-ops-agent on Cloud Run /a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json rather than /.well-known/agent-card.json? Answer: In Python ADK projects scaffolded by agents-cli, fast_api_app.py mounts A2A routes per application directory under /a2a/{agent_directory}/.well-known/agent-card.json. Because support-ops-agent uses the default agent_directory: "app" (matching App(name="app")), its card path is /a2a/app/.well-known/agent-card.json (whereas ADK Go scaffolds mount /.well-known/agent-card.json at the root). How do Gemini Enterprise's Agent Gallery and Google Cloud Agent Registry (gcloud agent-registry) complement each other in a large enterprise? Answer: The Agent Gallery (agents-cli publish gemini) is the workspace consumption portal where authorized employees discover and chat with approved assistants inside a specific Gemini Enterprise app. Google Cloud Agent Registry (gcloud agent-registry) is the cloud platform governance plane where architects and security teams inventory, describe, and audit all deployed agents (auto-registered from Agent Runtime) and MCP tool servers (toolspec.json) across projects and regions.

Welcome to Part 7: Capstone Project & Best Practices, and the first of the two capstone-scale projects that close out the course. This is your first real chance to put nearly everything you've learned so far to work in one system: multi-agent orchestration, distributed A2A, state, tools, and multimodal input. In this advanced module, we'll build a sophisticated AI agent capable of navigating a simulated e-commerce website to help a user find and purchase a product. This agent will demonstrate how to integrate external web environments and use a combination of tools to perform complex, multi-step tasks.

Figure: Distributed multi-agent shopping topology with orchestrator, personalization memory, and web browsing tool agent. The personalized shopping agent is a distributed multi-agent system composed of three specialized agents communicating via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol: Orchestrator Agent: The main, user-facing agent. It manages the conversation, understands user intent (including multimodal image input), and delegates tasks to the appropriate specialist. Personalization Agent: A remote agent responsible for managing user preferences. It uses the ADK's state management features to remember information like preferred sizes, colors, and brands. Known limitation: this persistence works reliably when you call personalization_agent directly, but it does not currently persist across separate turns of the orchestrator_agent in this lab's mandated architecture (AgentTool wrapping RemoteA2aAgent) — see "Known Limitation: Preferences Don't Persist Across Orchestrator Turns" below. Web Agent: A remote agent that acts as an interface to the e-commerce website. It exposes search/click as plain FunctionTool-wrapped Python functions, abstracting the web environment from the main orchestrator.

Web Environment: The agent interacts with a small, self-contained mock catalog (webshop_data.py) vendored directly in this lab's own web_agent project — a handful of in-memory products with an id, name, category, price, and description, plus a tiny in-process "session" tracking the currently viewed product. This stands in for a real e-commerce backend without requiring any extra install: the real web_agent_site Gym environment used by Google's personalized-shopping ADK sample pulls in a heavyweight dependency chain (pyserini, torch, spacy, a multi-GB product dataset) that's disproportionate to what this lab is teaching, and the web_agent_site package itself doesn't exist on PyPI — see the Setup section in the lab for details. Tools: The agent is equipped with two primary tools, both plain Python functions wrapped in FunctionTool: search(keywords: str): Filters the mock catalog by keyword and returns a short text listing of matching products (id, name, price). click(button: str): Simulates clicking a product ID from the search results, or a navigation button ("Buy Now", "Back to Search"). It updates the tiny in-process session and returns a text description of the resulting page. Prompt Engineering: The agent's instruction prompt is crucial for its success. It defines a state machine-like flow that guides the agent through the shopping process: Initial Inquiry: Ask the user for the product they're looking for. Search Phase: Use the search tool and present the results. Product Exploration: Use the click tool to navigate to product details, descriptions, features, and reviews. Purchase Confirmation: Use the click tool to select options and confirm the purchase. Finalization: Inform the user that the purchase is complete. The prompt also includes specific instructions on how to handle the web environment's state, such as using the "< Prev" button to navigate back. Artifacts (optional extension): This lab's solution doesn't save artifacts — but the web_agent's click/search tools are a natural place to add tool_context.save_artifact() calls, saving the HTML content of the current page after each action. That would let a user see the web page the agent is interacting with in the ADK's web UI, using the same pattern from Module 23. By combining these components, we can create a powerful agent that can navigate a web environment, gather information, and interact with a user to complete a complex task.

This is a genuine, verified architectural constraint of the current ADK 2.14 A2A stack — worth understanding rather than hiding, since it's exactly the kind of real-world limitation you'll hit building distributed agent systems. What works: if you talk to personalization_agent directly (bypassing the orchestrator), save_preference on one turn and get_preferences on a later, separate turn of the same session correctly returns the saved value. State persistence itself is fine. What doesn't work: ask orchestrator_agent to save a preference on turn 1, then — in a separate turn of the same orchestrator session — ask it to retrieve that preference. It comes back empty, even though the orchestrator is wired exactly as this lab instructs (AgentTool wrapping RemoteA2aAgent). Why: AgentTool.run_async (in google/adk/tools/agent_tool.py) spins up a brand-new InMemorySessionService and a brand-new child session on every single invocation, then discards it as soon as the call returns. RemoteA2aAgent's mechanism for resuming the same remote A2A conversation walks that child session's ctx.session.events backward looking for a context_id stashed in a previous response's metadata (_construct_message_parts_from_session in google/adk/agents/remote_a2a_agent.py). Because the child session is thrown away after each AgentTool call, that event history — and the context_id inside it — never survives to the next orchestrator turn. Each new turn's call to personalization_agent therefore starts a fresh remote A2A context with no memory of the previous one. We looked for a supported fix in google-adk 2.14 and didn't find one for this exact architecture: AgentTool.__init__ takes no session/context-reuse parameter (only skip_summarization, include_plugins, propagate_grounding_metadata). RemoteA2aAgent.__init__ has no way to pin a fixed context_id; it only ever discovers one by reading session event history. Executing a remote A2A specialist via bare sub_agents=[...] instead of AgentTool performs a one-way transfer_to_agent handoff rather than returning control to the orchestrator within the same turn, breaking multi-specialist synthesis. Bottom line: if your application genuinely needs preferences to survive across orchestrator turns, don't rely on AgentTool + RemoteA2aAgent for it today. Either call personalization_agent directly for anything that must persist, or back personalization_agent's tools with an external user-keyed store (such as Firestore or Redis keyed by user_id) rather than transient A2A session state.

documents.t: This advanced challenge project integrates many concepts from the course: distributed multi-agent systems (A2A), state management, and tool abstraction. The architecture separates concerns into a main Orchestrator, a stateful Personalization Agent, and a Web Agent that abstracts the web environment. The agent's instruction is engineered to follow a state machine-like process, guiding it through the complex, multi-step task of navigating a website. Artifacts aren't wired up in this lab's solution, but they're a natural optional extension for visualizing the agent's interaction with the web environment (see above). Abstraction via FunctionTool: Abstracting the website behind plain search/click functions (rather than having the orchestrator reason about raw HTML or website internals directly) is a superior design because it simplifies the orchestrator's reasoning task. The LLM only needs to know about the search(keywords: str) and click(button: str) signatures, not the complex and messy details of how the webshop is actually implemented. This improves reliability and makes the system more maintainable, as changes to the web environment's internals only require updating the Web Agent's tool implementations, not the orchestrator. Observability via Callbacks: Using a before_tool_callback for logging separates the concern of observability from the agent's business logic. The orchestrator's core instruction remains focused on delegation, while the callback transparently intercepts and logs the action. This makes the system more maintainable, as the monitoring logic can be updated independently of the agent's reasoning. Advantages of Distributed Architecture: This distributed A2A architecture offers significant advantages over a monolithic agent. It allows for independent scalability (the Web Agent can be scaled separately if it's under heavy load), modular maintenance (changes to the website's logic only require updating the Web Agent), and reusability (the Personalization Agent could be reused by other agents in the organization). Known limitation — AgentTool resets remote A2A context every call: preferences saved via the orchestrator do not currently survive across separate orchestrator turns, because AgentTool creates and discards a fresh session on every invocation, which breaks RemoteA2aAgent's mechanism for resuming the same remote conversation. Direct calls to personalization_agent are unaffected. See "Known Limitation" above for the full explanation and what we checked for a fix.

In this advanced challenge lab, you will synthesize concepts from the entire course so far to build a distributed, multi-agent personalized shopping assistant. You will create three separate agents that collaborate using Agent-to-Agent (A2A) communication to provide a stateful, multimodal, and observable shopping experience.

A Google Cloud Project with billing enabled and the Vertex AI API enabled (or a GEMINI_API_KEY). gcloud CLI installed and authenticated (gcloud auth application-default login) if using Vertex AI. uv installed (uv add "google-adk[a2a]" uvicorn python-dotenv).

Environment setup: 1-Click Launch (Browser): Open in GitHub CodespacesOpen in Google Cloud Shell Local machine: If you're continuing the course in sequence, cd into the adk-training project you created in Module 2 and skip the block below -- your environment and dependencies already carry forward. If you're starting fresh at this module, create that project first: uv init adk-training --python 3.10 && cd adk-training uv add "google-adk>=2.1.0" python-dotenv DevContainer / Codespaces (Alternative): If you opened this repository in a DevContainer or GitHub Codespaces, Python 3.11, uv, gcloud, and all core ADK dependencies are pre-installed in your container environment. Create and enter the main workspace directory for this lab: mkdir -p capstone_shopping_system && cd capstone_shopping_system Inside capstone_shopping_system, you will create three sibling ADK agent packages: web_agent, personalization_agent, and orchestrator_agent. A note on the webshop backend: Google's own personalized-shopping ADK sample (under google/adk-samples) talks to a real webshop simulation via a vendored web_agent_site module — a Gym environment with its own search engine, HTML rendering, and a multi-GB product dataset. It is not a pip-installable package (pip install web_agent_site returns a 404 — it doesn't exist on PyPI), and its real dependency chain (pyserini, torch, torchvision, spacy, gdown, a JVM for the search index, ...) is disproportionate to what this lab is actually teaching: getting three ADK agents to cooperate over A2A. Instead, Exercise 1 below has you write a tiny, self-contained mock catalog directly inside your own web_agent project — no extra install, no external dataset. If you want to see the real thing (or swap it in later), browse the vendored module at personalized_shopping/shared_libraries/web_agent_site/ in that repo.

This agent will be the interface to the e-commerce website. Create the web_agent project from inside capstone_shopping_system: uv run adk create web_agent cd web_agent Install A2A dependencies and create requirements.txt: uv add "google-adk[a2a]" uvicorn python-dotenv printf "google-adk[a2a]
uvicorn
python-dotenv
" > requirements.txt (Always include the [a2a] extra on google-adk[a2a] so to_a2a() and RemoteA2aAgent have their required A2A dependencies.) Create .env file: echo "GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=1" > .env echo "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=<your_gcp_project>" >> .env echo "GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=us-central1" >> .env Replace <your_gcp_project> with your actual Google Cloud Project ID (or set GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=0 and GEMINI_API_KEY=<your_key>). Create webshop_data.py: a tiny, dependency-free in-memory product catalog. This is your mock webshop backend. """A minimal, dependency-free mock e-commerce catalog and session model.""" CATALOG = [ {"id": "P001", "name": "Floral Summer Dress", "category": "dresses", "price": 39.99, "description": "A flowy, floral-print summer dress in breathable cotton."}, {"id": "P002", "name": "Men's Running Shoes", "category": "shoes", "price": 79.99, "description": "Lightweight running shoes with a breathable mesh upper."}, {"id": "P003", "name": "Wireless Noise-Cancelling Headphones", "category": "electronics", "price": 199.99, "description": "Over-ear headphones with active noise cancellation and 30-hour battery life."}, {"id": "P004", "name": "Stainless Steel Water Bottle", "category": "home", "price": 24.99, "description": "Insulated 750ml water bottle, keeps drinks cold for 24 hours."}, {"id": "P005", "name": "Organic Cotton T-Shirt", "category": "tops", "price": 19.99, "description": "Soft, breathable organic cotton crew-neck t-shirt."}, ] # Tiny in-process "session" tracking the currently viewed product, so # `click` can react to what `search` just showed. _session_state = {"current_product": None} def get_product(product_id: str): return next((p for p in CATALOG if p["id"] == product_id), None) Create the tools/ subpackage (tools/__init__.py, tools/search.py, and tools/click.py): First create the tools/ package directory: mkdir -p tools && touch tools/__init__.py Your task is to implement search and click as plain Python functions over the mock catalog above — no OpenAPI spec, just two functions you'll wrap in FunctionTool in the next step. Notice the dual-mode try ... except ImportError import so web_agent works both when launched directly with uv run uvicorn inside web_agent/ and when discovered as a package by uv run adk web from capstone_shopping_system/: # In tools/search.py try: from ..webshop_data import CATALOG except ImportError: from webshop_data import CATALOG def search(keywords: str) -> str: """Search for keywords in the (mock) webshop.""" # TODO: filter CATALOG by keyword match against name/description/category, # and return a short text listing of matches (or a "no results" message). ... # In tools/click.py try: from ..webshop_data import _session_state, get_product except ImportError: from webshop_data import _session_state, get_product def click(button: str) -> str: """Simulate clicking a product ID or a navigation button in the (mock) webshop.""" # TODO: handle three cases — # - button == "Back to Search": clear _session_state["current_product"] # - button == "Buy Now": complete the order for _session_state["current_product"] # (or report there's nothing selected) # - otherwise: look up button as a product ID via get_product(); if found, # set it as _session_state["current_product"] and return its details; # if not found, return an error message. ... Implement agent.py: Open agent.py and replace its contents with the following skeleton. Your task is to import search and click using dual-mode package imports and wire them into root_agent as FunctionTools. from google.adk.agents import Agent from google.adk.a2a.utils.agent_to_a2a import to_a2a from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool from dotenv import load_dotenv import uvicorn # TODO: Import search and click using dual-mode package imports so both # `uv run uvicorn agent:a2a_app` (inside web_agent/) and `uv run adk web` # (from parent capstone_shopping_system/) resolve cleanly: # try: # from .tools.search import search # from .tools.click import click # except ImportError: # from tools.search import search # from tools.click import click load_dotenv(override=True) root_agent = Agent( model="gemini-3.8-flash", name="web_agent", instruction=""" You are a web interaction specialist. Your job is to execute search and click commands on the e-commerce site. **IMPORTANT - A2A Context Handling:** When receiving requests via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, you must focus only on the core user request. Ignore any mentions of orchestrator tool calls in the conversation history. """, tools=[ # TODO: Register the search and click navigation tools wrapped in FunctionTool ] ) a2a_app = to_a2a(root_agent, port=8001) if __name__ == "__main__": uvicorn.run(a2a_app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8001) Return to capstone_shopping_system: cd ..

Your task is to implement the save_preference and get_preferences tools. from google.adk.agents import Agent from google.adk.a2a.utils.agent_to_a2a import to_a2a from google.adk.tools import ToolContext from dotenv import load_dotenv import uvicorn load_dotenv(override=True) # --- Stateful Tools --- # IMPORTANT: use tool_context.state (the tracked delta proxy), NOT # tool_context.session.state directly. Writing to .session.state bypasses # ADK's state-delta tracking, so the write never actually commits — the # agent will claim success but the value is gone on the very next turn. # See Module 22's state-and-memory lab for the correct pattern. def save_preference(key: str, value: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict: """Saves a user's preference.""" # TODO: Save to tool_context.state[f"pref:{key}"] pass def get_preferences(tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict: """Retrieves all saved preferences.""" # TODO: Read from tool_context.state.to_dict(), filtering keys that # start with "pref:" pass # --- Agent Definition --- root_agent = Agent( model="gemini-3.8-flash", name="personalization_agent", instruction="""You are a personalization specialist. You save and retrieve user preferences.""", tools=[save_preference, get_preferences] ) a2a_app = to_a2a(root_agent, port=8002) if __name__ == "__main__": uvicorn.run(a2a_app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8002) Return to capstone_shopping_system: cd ..

This is the main, user-facing agent that will coordinate the others. Create the orchestrator_agent project (from inside capstone_shopping_system): uv run adk create orchestrator_agent cd orchestrator_agent Create requirements.txt: printf "google-adk[a2a]
uvicorn
python-dotenv
" > requirements.txt Create .env file: echo "GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=1" > .env echo "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=<your_gcp_project>" >> .env echo "GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=us-central1" >> .env Replace <your_gcp_project> with your actual Google Cloud Project ID. Implement agent.py: Open agent.py and replace its contents with the following skeleton. Your task is to define the RemoteA2aAgent instances and complete the root_agent definition. Important: wire the two remote agents in as AgentTools (tools=[...]), not as sub_agents=[...]. sub_agents wires ADK's transfer_to_agent mechanism, which is a permanent, one-way handoff — once the orchestrator transfers control to one remote agent, it can never call the other remote agent or regain control to combine their results. AgentTool gives proper call-and-return semantics: the orchestrator calls each remote agent like a function, gets its result back, and stays in control to make the next call and synthesize a final combined answer — exactly what a multi-step instruction like "check preferences, then search the web" requires. from typing import Any, Dict, Optional from google.adk.agents import Agent from google.adk.agents.remote_a2a_agent import RemoteA2aAgent, AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH from google.adk.apps import App from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner from google.adk.tools import ToolContext from google.adk.tools.agent_tool import AgentTool from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv(override=True) # TODO: 1. Define remote specialist nodes # Instantiate RemoteA2aAgent for web_specialist (port 8001) and personalization_specialist (port 8002) # Pass use_legacy=False on both! web_specialist = ... personalization_specialist = ... # TODO: 2. Write a before_tool_callback that logs the name of the tool # being called (tool.name) every time the orchestrator delegates to a # specialist. It should never block the call -- always return None. def log_delegation(tool: BaseTool, args: Dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]: ... # TODO: 3. Define the main Orchestrator Agent. # Wire web_specialist and personalization_specialist in as AgentTools # (tools=[AgentTool(agent=...), AgentTool(agent=...)]), NOT as sub_agents=[...] — see the note above. # Register log_delegation as the agent's before_tool_callback. root_agent = Agent( model="gemini-3.8-flash", name="shopping_orchestrator", instruction="""You are a master shopping assistant. Coordinate with specialists.""", before_tool_callback=..., tools=[...] ) # Align App.name with the package directory name ("orchestrator_agent") # because ADK 2.14's AgentLoader loads module.app before module.root_agent. app = App(name="orchestrator_agent", root_agent=root_agent) runner = InMemoryRunner(app=app) Return to capstone_shopping_system: cd .. Known limitation to observe: once you get to "Running the System" below, try this: ask the orchestrator to save a preference, then — in a separate follow-up message of the same conversation — ask it what preferences it has saved for you. You'll find it comes back empty, even though the exact same request sent straight to personalization_agent (bypassing the orchestrator) works fine across turns. This is a real, verified limitation of the current ADK 2.14 A2A stack, not a bug in your code: AgentTool creates and discards a brand-new session on every single call, which breaks RemoteA2aAgent's mechanism for resuming the same remote conversation (it looks for context left behind in session history that no longer exists by the next turn). See the README's "Known Limitation" section for the full technical explanation. It's worth understanding this kind of constraint — distributed multi-agent systems have real seams like this one.

Enhance the Orchestrator to handle image-based searches. Challenge: Update the Orchestrator's instruction prompt. Add logic to handle image uploads. If a user provides an image, instruct the agent to: a. First, describe the item in the image. b. Then, use that text description to perform a search by delegating to the web_agent.

Plan how you would deploy this distributed system. Challenge: Create a Dockerfile for the web_agent. This file should define the steps to build a container image for your remote agent. Create a deployment_plan.md file. In this file, briefly explain the steps you would take to deploy the orchestrator_agent, web_agent, and personalization_agent as separate services on Google Cloud Run.

To test your full system, run the two remote A2A servers and launch the ADK Dev UI from the parent capstone_shopping_system directory in three separate terminals: Terminal 1 (web_agent): cd capstone_shopping_system/web_agent && uv run uvicorn agent:a2a_app --host localhost --port 8001 Terminal 2 (personalization_agent): cd capstone_shopping_system/personalization_agent && uv run uvicorn agent:a2a_app --host localhost --port 8002 Terminal 3 (orchestrator_agent, from parent directory): cd capstone_shopping_system && uv run adk web Select orchestrator_agent in the Dev UI dropdown, interact with the Orchestrator, and use the Trace view to observe the A2A communication and delegation.

This is a complex lab with multiple deployments. It is crucial to delete the resources you created after completing the lab. For Local Development:​ Stop all running uvicorn and uv run adk web processes (Ctrl+C in each terminal). Delete the capstone_shopping_system directory: cd .. rm -rf capstone_shopping_system For Cloud Deployments (if you completed Exercise 5):​ Delete Cloud Run Services: gcloud run services delete web-agent-service --region=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION --async gcloud run services delete personalization-agent-service --region=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION --async gcloud run services delete orchestrator-agent-service --region=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION --async Delete Artifact Registry Repository: gcloud artifacts repositories delete adk-images --location=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION --async Delete the GitHub Repository: If you used agents-cli to scaffold deployment, delete the GitHub repository you created.

This system uses three separate agents. What are the advantages of this distributed architecture in terms of scalability, maintainability, and reusability? The orchestrator_agent uses a before_tool_callback for logging. How does this separate the concern of observability from the agent's core business logic? The web_agent abstracts the website behind plain search/click functions. Why is this a better design than having the orchestrator directly interact with the raw HTML (or internal implementation) of the website? You observed that preferences don't survive across separate orchestrator turns, even though the same request sent directly to personalization_agent works. Walk through why, in terms of what AgentTool does to the session on every call. What would you need to change about the wiring (not just the prompt) to fix it?

This solution provides the complete, tested code for the distributed, multi-agent personalized shopping assistant. It demonstrates the definitive ADK 2.0 A2A pattern.

A minimal, dependency-free mock e-commerce catalog standing in for a real webshop, so web_agent's search/click tools have something to operate on without any extra install step. """A minimal, dependency-free mock e-commerce catalog and session model.""" CATALOG = [ { "id": "P001", "name": "Floral Summer Dress", "category": "dresses", "price": 39.99, "description": "A flowy, floral-print summer dress in breathable cotton.", }, { "id": "P002", "name": "Men's Running Shoes", "category": "shoes", "price": 79.99, "description": "Lightweight running shoes with a breathable mesh upper.", }, { "id": "P003", "name": "Wireless Noise-Cancelling Headphones", "category": "electronics", "price": 199.99, "description": "Over-ear headphones with active noise cancellation and 30-hour battery life.", }, { "id": "P004", "name": "Stainless Steel Water Bottle", "category": "home", "price": 24.99, "description": "Insulated 750ml water bottle, keeps drinks cold for 24 hours.", }, { "id": "P005", "name": "Organic Cotton T-Shirt", "category": "tops", "price": 19.99, "description": "Soft, breathable organic cotton crew-neck t-shirt.", }, ] # Tiny in-process "session" tracking the currently viewed product, so # `click` can react to what `search` just showed. _session_state = {"current_product": None} def get_product(product_id: str): return next((p for p in CATALOG if p["id"] == product_id), None)

try: from ..webshop_data import CATALOG except ImportError: from webshop_data import CATALOG def search(keywords: str) -> str: """Search for keywords in the (mock) webshop.""" terms = keywords.lower().split() matches = [ p for p in CATALOG if any( t in p["name"].lower() or t in p["description"].lower() or t in p["category"].lower() for t in terms ) ] if not matches: return "No products found matching your search. Try different keywords." lines = [f"Found {len(matches)} product(s):"] for p in matches: lines.append(f"- [{p['id']}] {p['name']} — ${p['price']:.2f}") return "\n".join(lines)

try: from ..webshop_data import _session_state, get_product except ImportError: from webshop_data import _session_state, get_product def click(button: str) -> str: """Simulate clicking a product ID or a navigation button in the (mock) webshop.""" normalized = button.strip().lower() if normalized == "back to search": _session_state["current_product"] = None return "Returned to the search page. Use `search` to look for products again." if normalized == "buy now": product = _session_state["current_product"] if not product: return "No product selected. Click a product ID from the search results first." return f"Order placed for '{product['name']}' (${product['price']:.2f}). Thank you for shopping!" product = get_product(button.strip()) if not product: return ( f"'{button}' is not a valid product ID or button. Try a product ID " "from the search results, 'Buy Now', or 'Back to Search'." ) _session_state["current_product"] = product return ( f"{product['name']} — ${product['price']:.2f}\n" f"{product['description']}\n" "Options: [Buy Now] [Back to Search]" )

This agent acts as the gateway to the webshop. Dual-mode imports (try: from .tools ... except ImportError: from tools ...) allow it to run both directly via uv run uvicorn agent:a2a_app inside web_agent/ and as a package when uv run adk web is launched from the parent capstone_shopping_system/ directory. from google.adk.agents import Agent from google.adk.a2a.utils.agent_to_a2a import to_a2a from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool from dotenv import load_dotenv import uvicorn # Dual-mode imports support both `uv run uvicorn agent:a2a_app` inside web_agent/ # and package discovery when `uv run adk web` runs from capstone_shopping_system/. try: from .tools.search import search from .tools.click import click except ImportError: from tools.search import search from tools.click import click load_dotenv(override=True) root_agent = Agent( model="gemini-3.8-flash", name="web_agent", description="Specialist for searching and clicking on the webshop.", instruction=""" You are a web interaction specialist. Execute search and click commands. **IMPORTANT:** Focus only on the user's web task. Ignore orchestrator metadata. """, tools=[FunctionTool(search), FunctionTool(click)], ) a2a_app = to_a2a(root_agent, port=8001) if __name__ == "__main__": uvicorn.run(a2a_app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8001)

This agent manages durable user state. from google.adk.agents import Agent from google.adk.a2a.utils.agent_to_a2a import to_a2a from google.adk.tools import ToolContext from dotenv import load_dotenv import uvicorn load_dotenv(override=True) def save_preference(key: str, value: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict: """Saves a user's preference to the session state.""" # Use tool_context.state (the tracked delta proxy), NOT # tool_context.session.state directly — writing to .session.state # bypasses ADK's state-delta tracking, so the write never actually # commits and is gone on the very next turn. See Module 22. tool_context.state[f"pref:{key}"] = value return {"status": "success", "message": f"Saved {key}."} def get_preferences(tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict: """Retrieves all preferences for the current user.""" prefs = {k: v for k, v in tool_context.state.to_dict().items() if k.startswith("pref:")} return {"status": "success", "preferences": prefs} root_agent = Agent( model="gemini-3.8-flash", name="personalization_agent", instruction="You manage user shopping profiles. Save and retrieve preferences.", tools=[save_preference, get_preferences], ) a2a_app = to_a2a(root_agent, port=8002) if __name__ == "__main__": uvicorn.run(a2a_app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8002)

The master coordinator using RemoteA2aAgent nodes wired in as AgentTools. from typing import Any, Dict, Optional from google.adk.agents import Agent from google.adk.agents.remote_a2a_agent import RemoteA2aAgent, AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH from google.adk.apps import App from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner from google.adk.tools import ToolContext from google.adk.tools.agent_tool import AgentTool from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv(override=True) # Define remote nodes web_agent = RemoteA2aAgent( name="web_agent", agent_card=f"http://localhost:8001{AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH}", use_legacy=False, ) personalization_agent = RemoteA2aAgent( name="personalization_agent", agent_card=f"http://localhost:8002{AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH}", use_legacy=False, ) def log_delegation(tool: BaseTool, args: Dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]: """AgentOps: logs every delegation to a remote specialist. This is pure observability -- it never blocks or alters the call (always returns None), so it can be added, changed, or removed without touching the orchestrator's instruction or reasoning at all.""" print(f"[DELEGATION] shopping_orchestrator -> {tool.name}") return None # Orchestrator root_agent = Agent( model="gemini-3.8-flash", name="shopping_orchestrator", instruction=""" You are a master assistant. 1. Check preferences via `personalization_agent`. 2. Search web via `web_agent`. 3. Help user checkout. """, # NOTE: these two remote agents are wired as tools (AgentTool), NOT as # `sub_agents=[...]`. `sub_agents` wires ADK's `transfer_to_agent` # mechanism, and for a RemoteA2aAgent that mechanism is a one-way handoff # within the turn: RemoteA2aAgent runs in a separate process with no # knowledge of the orchestrator or sibling specialists, so it cannot # transfer onward to `web_agent` or hand control back to synthesize a # combined answer. `AgentTool` gives clean call-and-return semantics: # the orchestrator calls each remote agent like a function, gets its # result back, and stays in control across multiple calls. # # KNOWN LIMITATION (verified in google-adk 2.14): AgentTool.run_async # spins up a brand-new InMemorySessionService + child session on *every* # call and discards it immediately after. RemoteA2aAgent resumes a prior # remote A2A conversation by walking that child session's event history # backward for a previously-stored context_id -- history that no longer # exists on the next orchestrator turn. Consequently, preferences saved # via the orchestrator on turn 1 do not persist to a separate turn 2 via # the orchestrator, even though hitting `personalization_agent` directly # persists across turns. See the README's "Known Limitation" section. tools=[AgentTool(agent=web_agent), AgentTool(agent=personalization_agent)], before_tool_callback=log_delegation, ) # IMPORTANT (ADK 2.14 AgentLoader behavior): When `uv run adk web` runs from # the parent `capstone_shopping_system/` directory, ADK's `AgentLoader` checks # for a module-level `app` (`isinstance(module.app, App)`) BEFORE falling back # to `root_agent`. Always align `App(name="orchestrator_agent", ...)` with the # package directory name (`orchestrator_agent`) so both `uv run adk web` and # programmatic `InMemoryRunner(app=app)` sessions resolve the same `app_name`. app = App(name="orchestrator_agent", root_agent=root_agent) runner = InMemoryRunner(app=app)

The only change needed is to the orchestrator's instruction -- Gemini's multimodal input handling and AgentTool's text-only interface to the remote web_agent do the rest. When the incoming message contains an image part, the orchestrator describes what it sees in plain text, then passes that description as the keywords argument of its web_agent delegation (remember, AgentTool always sends a single text request to the remote agent -- images themselves are never forwarded, only the orchestrator's description of them). Replace the orchestrator's instruction from Exercise 3 with: instruction=""" You are a master shopping assistant. Coordinate with specialists. 1. Check preferences via `personalization_agent` when relevant. 2. If the user's message includes an image, first describe the item shown in the image in a short, plain-text phrase (its type, color, and style -- e.g. "blue athletic running shoe"). Then use that text description as the `keywords` for a search delegated to `web_agent`. Do not ask the user to describe the image themselves -- describe it yourself and search directly. 3. Otherwise, search the web via `web_agent` using the user's text description directly. 4. Help the user checkout. """, Verified live: sending a synthetic PNG of a blue running-shoe silhouette (no text hint about what it was, just "I want to buy something like this. Can you find it?") produced this real trace: CALL web_agent({'request': 'blue athletic running shoe'}) [DELEGATION] shopping_orchestrator -> web_agent RESP web_agent -> "I found a pair of Men's Running Shoes for $79.99. ..." FINAL: I found a pair of Men's Running Shoes for $79.99. Would you like to add them to your cart, or are you looking for something else? The orchestrator described the image itself, delegated a text search to web_agent, and matched a real catalog item (P002) -- exactly the flow Exercise 4 asks for. To try it yourself, send a types.Content with two parts to the orchestrator's runner: an image part (types.Part.from_bytes(data=image_bytes, mime_type="image/png")) and a text part, in the same message.

web_agent/Dockerfile: FROM python:3.11-slim WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt COPY . . # Cloud Run injects $PORT; to_a2a()'s own port=8001 argument only matters # for local `python agent.py` runs, so bind uvicorn to $PORT here instead. ENV PORT=8080 EXPOSE 8080 CMD ["sh", "-c", "uvicorn agent:a2a_app --host 0.0.0.0 --port ${PORT}"] The same Dockerfile (copied into each agent's own directory) works unchanged for personalization_agent and orchestrator_agent too -- only the module path (agent:a2a_app) and each project's own requirements.txt differ, and the orchestrator doesn't expose an a2a_app/port at all when run via adk web/adk api_server in production instead of a raw uvicorn command. deployment_plan.md: # Deployment Plan: Distributed Shopping Agent System ## Overview Three independent Cloud Run services, deployed and scaled separately, talking to each other over HTTPS via the A2A protocol. ## 1. Build and push images For each of `web_agent`, `personalization_agent`, `orchestrator_agent` (ensure `requirements.txt` includes `google-adk[a2a]` and `uvicorn`): gcloud artifacts repositories create adk-images \ --repository-format=docker --location=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION gcloud builds submit ./web_agent \ --tag $GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION-docker.pkg.dev/$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT/adk-images/web-agent (repeat for personalization_agent and orchestrator_agent) ## 2. Deploy web_agent and personalization_agent first They have no dependencies on each other or on the orchestrator: gcloud run deploy web-agent-service \ --image=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION-docker.pkg.dev/$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT/adk-images/web-agent \ --region=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION --no-allow-unauthenticated \ --set-env-vars=GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=1,GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT,GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION (repeat for personalization-agent-service) Use `--no-allow-unauthenticated`: these are internal specialist agents, not user-facing endpoints. Grant the orchestrator's own Cloud Run service account the `roles/run.invoker` role on both, and use `google.auth` / an ID-token-fetching `httpx_client` when constructing each `RemoteA2aAgent` in production, instead of the lab's unauthenticated `localhost` URLs. ## 3. Point the orchestrator at the deployed URLs Update `orchestrator_agent/agent.py` so `web_agent`'s and `personalization_agent`'s `agent_card` URLs point at their Cloud Run service URLs (from step 2's deploy output) instead of `localhost:8001` / `localhost:8002`, then deploy the orchestrator the same way -- this one *can* be `--allow-unauthenticated` (or fronted by IAP/your own auth) since it's the user-facing entry point: gcloud run deploy orchestrator-agent-service \ --image=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION-docker.pkg.dev/$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT/adk-images/orchestrator-agent \ --region=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION --allow-unauthenticated \ --set-env-vars=GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=1,GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT,GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=$GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION ## 4. Scale independently Set `--min-instances`/`--max-instances` per service based on load: e.g. `web_agent` may need more replicas than `personalization_agent` if search traffic dominates over preference lookups -- this is the "independent scalability" benefit called out in the Self-Reflection answers. ## 5. Observability `orchestrator_agent`'s `log_delegation` callback currently `print`s to stdout; on Cloud Run that's captured automatically by Cloud Logging, so no code change is required to get delegation events into GCP's logging pipeline -- only a change of sink is needed if you want somewhere other than the default Cloud Run log destination. ## Known gap to flag before going further than this lab This plan does not address the cross-turn preference persistence limitation documented in the README/Exercise 3 comments above -- deploying to Cloud Run does not change that behavior, since it's caused by `AgentTool`'s in-process session handling regardless of where the processes run.

This system uses three separate agents. What are the advantages of this distributed architecture in terms of scalability, maintainability, and reusability? Scalability: Each agent can be deployed and scaled independently (e.g. 10 instances of web_agent for 1 instance of personalization_agent). Maintainability: Changes to the website's logic only require updating web_agent -- the orchestrator and personalization_agent are untouched. Reusability: Other apps in the organization could call the same personalization_agent endpoint instead of reimplementing preference storage. The orchestrator_agent uses a before_tool_callback for logging. How does this separate the concern of observability from the agent's core business logic? Answer: log_delegation never appears in the orchestrator's instruction and never changes what the orchestrator decides to do -- it always returns None, so the tool call proceeds exactly as the LLM requested. It's registered once on the Agent and fires automatically before every tool call, including calls to web_agent/personalization_agent that the model decides to make on its own. You could delete the callback entirely (or swap it for something that writes to Cloud Logging instead of print) without touching the instruction or the delegation logic at all -- observability and business logic evolve independently. The web_agent abstracts the website behind plain search/click functions. Why is this a better design than having the orchestrator directly interact with the raw HTML (or internal implementation) of the website? Answer: The orchestrator only ever needs to reason about two simple signatures, search(keywords: str) and click(button: str) -- not HTML parsing, CSS selectors, or the mock catalog's internal data structures. If the website's implementation changes (a real backend replaces the mock catalog, or the HTML structure changes), only web_agent's tool implementations need to change; the orchestrator's instruction and reasoning are completely unaffected. This is the same separation-of-concerns benefit as OpenAPIToolset in Module 11, applied at the level of a whole remote agent instead of a single tool. You observed that preferences don't survive across separate orchestrator turns, even though the same request sent directly to personalization_agent works. Walk through why, in terms of what AgentTool does to the session on every call. What would you need to change about the wiring (not just the prompt) to fix it? Answer: AgentTool.run_async creates a fresh InMemorySessionService and a brand-new child session on every call, then throws it away as soon as the call returns. RemoteA2aAgent figures out whether it's continuing a previous remote conversation by scanning that session's event history backward for a context_id left in a prior response's metadata. Because the child session is discarded after each AgentTool call, there is no event history left for the next orchestrator turn to search -- so RemoteA2aAgent always starts a brand-new remote A2A context, and the remote agent (which itself has correct, working state persistence) never gets asked about the earlier conversation. No prompt change fixes this, because the LLM never sees or controls session lifecycle -- it's a framework-level behavior in AgentTool.run_async and RemoteA2aAgent._construct_message_parts_from_session. A real fix requires either reusing a persistent child session/context across calls (not exposed as a built-in parameter on AgentTool in ADK 2.14) or storing user preferences in an external database keyed by user_id (such as Firestore or Redis) rather than transient A2A session state.

Building a working agent is the first step. Building a production-ready agent requires a focus on architecture, performance, security, and reliability. This module summarizes the essential best practices for taking your agent from a prototype to a robust, scalable, and maintainable application, aligned with the ADK 2.0 Workflow Runtime. Figure: Defense-in-depth architecture covering input validation, execution resilience, state integrity, and observability.

In ADK 2.0, every component is a Node in a Workflow Graph. Choosing the right structure is your most critical design decision. Pattern When to use it Key Characteristics Agent Natural language reasoning and dynamic tool calling. Non-deterministic, flexible. Best for high-level decision making. Workflow (Static) Fixed, predictable pipelines (Sequential/Parallel). Deterministic. Reduced latency and cost by avoiding LLM routing where logic is known. @node (Dynamic) Complex, code-based orchestration (Loops, If/Else). Maximum control. Allows arbitrary Python logic between agent executions. Small, Focused Tools: Design your tools to follow the single-responsibility principle. A tool should do one thing well. Progressive Disclosure with Skills: Don't overload an agent with 50 tools. Group related domain workflows and instructions into Skills (SkillToolset, covered in depth in Module 39.5) and only activate them on demand when needed. Deterministic Routing: If you know that Step B always follows Step A, don't ask an LLM to decide. Use a Workflow or a Dynamic @node.

documents.t: ADK 2.0 changes the way we handle failures. Instead of writing complex try...except logic inside every tool, we now leverage the Workflow Runtime. The "Let it Fail" Pattern​ In ADK 1.x, you were taught to catch all exceptions in tools. In ADK 2.0, you should allow standard exceptions to propagate out of your tools and workflow nodes. Why? Automatic Retries: If a node or tool fails with an exception, the ADK framework can automatically retry the execution based on a RetryConfig. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Interrupts: When a workflow pauses for human input, ADK unwinds the node stack using NodeInterruptedError. In ADK 2.14, NodeInterruptedError inherits directly from Python's BaseException (rather than Exception) specifically so normal except Exception: blocks won't accidentally catch it—however, never write a bare except: or except BaseException: without re-raising, as swallowing NodeInterruptedError silently breaks workflow pause and resume! Configuring Retries​ You configure retry logic per-node, on the node itself (either as a constructor argument like Agent(..., retry_config=...), or via @node(retry_config=...) for function nodes): from google.adk.workflow import RetryConfig # Framework handles retries for you! my_agent_node = Agent( ..., retry_config=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, initial_delay=2.0) ) Important: retry_config does not cascade from a container to the nodes inside it. Setting retry_config on a Workflow(...) only governs retries of that Workflow as a node (relevant if it's nested inside a parent graph) — it has no effect on the nodes in its own edges. If you want a specific node inside a Workflow to retry, put retry_config directly on that node.

Model Selection Hierarchy: Use gemini-3.8-flash for routing, classification, and simple tool calling. Save gemini-3.1-pro-preview for complex multi-step reasoning. Caching with before_agent_callback or Keyed Node Caches: Implement a caching layer keyed on the normalized user query to skip redundant LLM or backend calls when an identical request was recently processed. Async Everything: Always use async tool and node definitions to prevent blocking the event loop during I/O-bound tasks (API calls, DB queries).

Fail-Closed Validation: Use Pydantic schemas for input and output contracts. If validation fails, the entry node raises immediately, preventing prompt injection or malformed data from propagating downstream. Secrets Management: Use Google Secret Manager or .env files. Never log sensitive data or return it in an agent response. HITL for Side Effects: Any action that performs a destructive or irreversible side effect (deleting data, executing a financial transfer) must pause for human approval using the right primitive for your layer: Agent Tools (FunctionTool): Wrap standard Python tool functions with FunctionTool(my_fn, require_confirmation=True) (Module 13) so ADK automatically emits a confirmation RequestInput event before executing the tool. Workflow Nodes (@node): Inside a generator @node function, explicitly yield RequestInput(...) (from google.adk.events) to pause the workflow graph until the user supplies confirmation or structured input.

Think in Nodes: Break logic into discrete, testable nodes orchestrated by a Workflow, and pass validated domain payloads cleanly from node to node. Framework Resilience: Propagate exceptions to enable ADK 2.0 automatic retries, and never swallow BaseException / NodeInterruptedError. Model Efficiency: Match the model capability to the task complexity, and use Skills (Module 39.5) for progressive context disclosure. Strict Schemas & HITL: Use Pydantic to enforce "fail-closed" security at node boundaries and FunctionTool(..., require_confirmation=True) or @node yield RequestInput(...) for destructive side effects.

Pay close attention to data threading: validate_input_node and flaky_api_node must forward the validated query string (received via each @node's node_input: str pass-through parameter) so cache_node keys _slow_query(query) on the actual user query rather than on a constant status message! # In best_practices_v2/agent.py (Starter Code) import json import time import random import functools from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, constr from google.adk import Workflow from google.adk.workflow import node, RetryConfig # --- 1. Also note that # in ADK 2.14's default `@node` binding mode, the parameter named literally # `node_input` receives the upstream node's return value directly (whereas # differently named parameters are looked up in `ctx.state`). @node def validate_input_node(node_input: str) -> str: """Validates inputs using a Pydantic model and returns the validated query.""" # TODO 1: Parse node_input as JSON (json.loads). Wrap it in a try/except # json.JSONDecodeError and re-raise as a ValueError with a clear # "Malformed input" message (also check isinstance(payload, dict)). # TODO 2: Instantiate `validated = ValidatedInput(**payload)`. # If either step fails, an exception propagates and the workflow stops # immediately (Fail-Closed). # TODO 3: Return `validated.query` so downstream nodes receive the actual # user query string via `node_input`! pass # --- 2. Resilience with Framework-Level Retries --- # TODO: Add retry_config=RetryConfig(max_attempts=4) directly to @node(...)! @node async def flaky_api_node(node_input: str) -> str: """Simulates an API call that might fail transiently.""" query = node_input print(f"Attempting to call the flaky API for query={query!r}...") if random.random() > 0.33: # 67% chance of failure print("API call failed! Raising exception for framework retry...") # TODO: Raise a ConnectionError. DO NOT catch it here (and never use bare `except:`)! pass print("API call succeeded!") # TODO: Return `query` so `cache_node` receives the validated user query # (do NOT return a constant string, or every query will hit the same cache key!). pass # --- 3. Performance with Query-Keyed Caching --- @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128) def _slow_query(query: str) -> str: print(f"Performing slow backend query for: {query!r}...") time.sleep(2) return f"Verified results for '{query}'" @node def cache_node(node_input: str) -> str: # TODO: Pass `query = node_input` into `_slow_query(query)` and return # f"Cached Result: {result}". pass # --- 4. The Orchestrator Workflow --- # TODO: Define a Workflow wiring: # ("START", validate_input_node) -> (validate_input_node, flaky_api_node) -> (flaky_api_node, cache_node) # IMPORTANT: put `retry_config=RetryConfig(max_attempts=4)` directly on # `flaky_api_node`'s `@node(...)` decorator above, NOT on the `Workflow(...)` # container (`Workflow.retry_config` does NOT cascade to child nodes). root_agent = Workflow( name="BestPracticesSystem", edges=[ # ("START", validate_input_node), ... ] )

Navigate to the parent directory and start the Dev UI: cd .. uv run adk web Select best_practices_v2 in the Dev UI dropdown. Interact and Observe: Test Validation (Fail-Closed): Send a valid JSON payload matching ValidatedInput, such as {"user_id": "student_01", "query": "laptops"}. It should pass validation and proceed through the pipeline. Now test two malformed inputs and verify the Workflow halts immediately both times: Non-JSON text (e.g., hello) — rejected by your json.loads check with a clear ValueError. Schema-invalid JSON (e.g., {"user_id": "a", "query": "laptops"} where user_id is under 3 characters) — rejected by Pydantic's ValidationError. Test Retries: Watch your terminal logs when sending a valid JSON message. Whenever the 67% simulated failure triggers, you will see "Attempting to call the flaky API..." multiple times as the ADK Workflow Runtime automatically retries flaky_api_node. Test Per-Query Caching: Send {"user_id": "student_01", "query": "laptops"} once — notice "Performing slow backend query for: 'laptops'..." and the 2-second delay. Send the same {"user_id": "student_01", "query": "laptops"} again — once flaky_api_node succeeds, cache_node returns instantly without printing "Performing slow backend query..."! Now send a different query, {"user_id": "student_01", "query": "headphones"} — notice it triggers a fresh 2-second lookup because _slow_query is properly keyed on query.

Record this lab as completed in your study plan? ✓ Mark as Complete Lab 38 Solution: Building a Production-Ready Agent (ADK 2.0) Goal​ This file contains the complete code for the agent.py script in the Best Practices lab, utilizing the ADK 2.0 Workflow Runtime and native resilience features. best_practices_v2/agent.py​ import json import time import random import functools from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, constr from google.adk import Workflow from google.adk.workflow import node, RetryConfig # --- 1. Input Validation with Pydantic (Fail-Closed) --- class ValidatedInput(BaseModel): """A Pydantic model to validate incoming user payloads.""" user_id: constr(pattern=r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{3,50}$") query: str = Field(..., min_length=1, max_length=1000) @node def validate_input_node(node_input: str) -> str: """Validates inputs using a Pydantic model and forwards the validated query. The Workflow Runner always delivers the entry node's input as the raw user message coerced to `str` (never as a `dict`), so we parse it as JSON here first. A malformed JSON payload, or one that fails the ValidatedInput schema, raises — the workflow engine catches this and stops execution (Fail-Closed). Returning `validated.query` threads the actual user query through `node_input` along the downstream edges so caching is keyed per query rather than on a constant status string. """ try: payload = json.loads(node_input) except json.JSONDecodeError as e: raise ValueError( f"Malformed input: expected a JSON object, got: {node_input!r}" ) from e if not isinstance(payload, dict): raise ValueError( f"Malformed input: expected a JSON object mapping, got: {type(payload).__name__}" ) # Instantiating the model raises a ValidationError if inputs are invalid. validated = ValidatedInput(**payload) return validated.query # --- 2. Resilience with Framework-Level Retries --- # NOTE on @node parameter binding in ADK 2.14: in default binding mode, the # parameter named literally `node_input` receives the upstream node's return # value (`validated.query`) directly, whereas any other parameter name would # be looked up in `ctx.state`. Keep `node_input: str` here to receive the # validated query string cleanly! @node(retry_config=RetryConfig(max_attempts=4)) async def flaky_api_node(node_input: str) -> str: """Simulates an upstream API pre-check that might fail transiently.""" query = node_input print(f"Attempting to call the flaky API for query={query!r}...") if random.random() > 0.33: # 67% chance of transient failure print("API call failed! Raising exception for framework retry...") # Propagate standard exceptions — NEVER catch them here or use bare `except:`. raise ConnectionError("The external API is temporarily unavailable.") print("API call succeeded!") # Forward the validated `query` so `cache_node` caches per actual user query! return query # --- 3. Performance with Query-Keyed Caching --- @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128) def _slow_query(query: str) -> str: """A deterministic backend lookup with per-query in-memory LRU caching.""" print(f"Performing slow backend query for: {query!r}...") time.sleep(2) # Simulate expensive I/O latency on cache miss return f"Verified results for '{query}'" @node def cache_node(node_input: str) -> str: """Executes the query through the LRU cache keyed by the user's `query`.""" query = node_input result = _slow_query(query) return f"Cached Result: {result}" # --- 4. The Orchestrator Workflow --- # Assemble the components into a deterministic Graph: # START -> validate_input_node (extracts `query`) -> flaky_api_node (retries, forwards `query`) -> cache_node (`_slow_query(query)`) root_agent = Workflow( name="BestPracticesSystem", edges=[ ("START", validate_input_node), (validate_input_node, flaky_api_node), (flaky_api_node, cache_node), ], # NOTE: retry_config is set on `flaky_api_node` itself (above), not here. # `Workflow` extends `BaseNode`, so it accepts `retry_config` too — but # that only governs retries of the Workflow *as a node* (if nested inside # a parent graph). It does NOT cascade to the nodes inside its own graph. ) Key Takeaways Explained​ Fail-Closed Security & Clean Data Threading: By validating JSON at the entry node with Pydantic and returning validated.query, malformed payloads halt immediately while valid requests pass the clean query string downstream via each @node's node_input: str pass-through parameter. Native Resilience: ADK 2.0's RetryConfig separates business logic from error handling. Nodes stay clean without manual retry loops, and avoiding bare except: ensures both ConnectionError retries and NodeInterruptedError (BaseException) HITL pauses work seamlessly. Per-Query Caching: Because validate_input_node and flaky_api_node forward query rather than a static string, _slow_query(query) caches results per distinct user query—giving an instant cache hit when repeating "laptops" while still computing fresh results for "headphones". Deterministic Routing: Using a Workflow graph instead of an LLM router for fixed pipelines eliminates unnecessary token cost and routing latency. Self-Reflection Answers​ Why is it better to let the framework handle retries rather than writing manual loops in your tool functions? Answer: Centralized retry logic ensures consistent behavior across all nodes, surfaces every retry attempt in ADK's Trace View for debugging, and lets you tune backoff policy declaratively via RetryConfig without cluttering business logic. What happens if you catch the exception inside flaky_api_node with a try/except block and return an error string? Does the framework still retry? Answer: No. The framework only triggers RetryConfig if an unhandled exception escapes the node. Catching it and returning a string marks the node run as "Successful" and passes that error string straight into cache_node (which would even poison your cache with the error message!). In a production environment (like Cloud Run), why is lru_cache only a partial solution for performance? Answer: Cloud Run is serverless and scales horizontally across isolated container instances. functools.lru_cache lives only in one process's RAM—if Request 1 lands on Instance A and Request 2 lands on Instance B (or Instance A scales to zero), the cache misses. Production multi-instance deployments use a shared distributed cache like Google Cloud Memorystore for Redis.
